# messageHistoryMaxS Parameter Code Walkthrough

This page was originally intended to help people get back to the parameter from a stable filename, not to explain the entire logging setup. `src/cli/logging.go` is still the entry point: it is in the `cli` package, and the file starts with an import block; this ordinary location information actually holds up better on rechecking than the statement in the old notes that "the log object handles everything."

The early notes collapsed the concept of message history, the parameter name, and the point where the value is ultimately consumed into a single thing. The text from that time is still below. It is retained not because its conclusions still hold, but because people may reach this page through old links and use it to understand why the reading order later changed.

## Original Description of the Entry Point

> messageHistoryMaxS is the entry point for the limit on historical messages stored inside logging.go, and callers do not need to concern themselves with this value.

This claim was later narrowed. It mistook "where the parameter is received" for "the only place where the value takes effect." The only starting points that can be confirmed from this file are the code around the parameter and the immediately adjacent handoff; `package cli`, the import block, and the filename alone do not justify presenting the downstream object relationships as the only possible implementation.

The old page also had a habit of jumping straight to a likely log object whenever a logging-related name appeared. That made for quick reading, but missed whether the parameter value first passed through a default value, a local variable, or an initialization branch. For messageHistoryMaxS, breaking down the parameter's entry point first keeps the later path from being skewed by associations with its name.

## The Reading Method Still in Use

Start in `src/cli/logging.go`, at the first occurrence of `messageHistoryMaxS`. The first occurrence can only tell you how it enters the command-line layer: a declaration, a point where an option is received, a default value, or code adjacent to one of these locations. Do not decide at this stage exactly what stores the message history.

Next, look at where the same section of code puts the value locally. Distinguish between two kinds of lines here: those that merely turn an external parameter into a local value, and those that begin constructing or configuring downstream objects. The former identifies the entry point; only the latter provides names to follow further. When these two kinds of lines are close together, the old notes tended to merge them; this is precisely the correction this page needs to retain.

If the parameter name stops appearing at this point, do not conclude that it has no effect. Keep following the local variable that receives it until you reach an object or function call whose definition can be looked up independently. An object boundary is an appropriate stopping point: noting the boundary's name and then looking up its definition is more useful than repeatedly searching for the same parameter name in logging.go.

If the parameter name appears multiple times in the same file, do not immediately interpret every occurrence as a different path, either. First establish which ones are merely declarations, help text, or default values; only the handoffs after the value is actually obtained should go into the code-reading notes. The original draft did not make this distinction, so it also counted places where text appears as places where behavior occurs.

## Retained Review Addendum

The previous review already removed the claim about an "internal destination," but still left an inaccurate implication: that following the local variables in logging.go downward would necessarily yield the complete call chain. That implication should also be discarded. Reading within the file can only pin down the entry point and directly adjacent relationships; once you leave the file, whether the same semantics still hold depends on the definition and usage sites of the object the value is passed to.

The review sequence at the time was as follows, and is still useful for avoiding the same detours:

1. Find the first occurrence of `messageHistoryMaxS` and mark whether it is a receiving point or a default value.
2. Find where the value is actually obtained immediately afterward, and confirm whether it is renamed or wrapped in local configuration.
3. Follow only the nearest handoff, and stop when you encounter an independent object or function call.
4. When you need to cross files, continue from that object or call name, rather than making further inferences from the filename of logging.go.

This is not a complete logging troubleshooting procedure. It only gives readers an order for returning to the entry point, to avoid conflating parameter text, log objects, and runtime effects from the outset.

## About the Old Note

`DOC-11` is an adjacent old note on log code. It retains scattered names and impressions from the early reading, and is useful for comparison once you are already in the logging code; it does not prove the handoff relationships for messageHistoryMaxS. Previously, someone read the two pages together and treated "log" in the note as the parameter's final destination, precisely repeating this page's early mistake.

This page is still referenced because the entry path has not become any harder to find, not because the early explanation is still reliable. When rechecking this parameter, first locate three points within `src/cli/logging.go`: where the parameter appears, where it is received locally, and the first boundary where it crosses into another object. The old assessment goes no further than that boundary.

Finally, one question remains unexplored: whether the source of the default value is in the same initialization section as the point where the parameter is received. The original notes did not provide enough code snippets to support adding a conclusion; the next time you revisit the code, simply check this near the parameter's first occurrence.

## Flow That Can Already Be Confirmed Within the File

```text
Log(level, record)
  |
  +-- passthrough or CRITICAL
  |      `-- origBackend.Log(...) -> return
  |
  `-- interactive display path
         |-- formatter.Format -> TrimSpace
         |-- logMessages.PushBack
         |-- messageCount < messageHistoryMaxSize
         |      `-- messageHistory.PushBack
         |-- messageCount++
         `-- RecalcLines

GetMessageHistory
  `-- messageHistory.Front -> Next -> lineWrap -> []string
```

This diagram adds local relationships that can be checked line by line. `Log` begins by holding the mutex; in passthrough mode, or for `CRITICAL` records, it passes the records to `origBackend.Log` and returns immediately. The remaining records pass through formatter and `TrimSpace` before entering `logMessages`. Only when `messageCount` is still less than `messageHistoryMaxSize` does the same text also enter `messageHistory`; the count itself increments every time this path is taken.

Therefore, the history limit is not a CLI parameter passed in by the caller, but the `messageHistoryMaxSize = 100` constant within the file. `messageHistoryMaxS` in the old title is still retained as a truncated name for looking up old records, but the full identifier should be used when reviewing the source code. This also explains why "how many entries have been saved" and "how many entries have passed through in total" need to be considered separately: once the limit is reached, the list stops appending entries, while `messageCount` continues to increase.

`GetMessageHistory` reads the saved entries from the head of the linked list to the tail, calls `lineWrap` on each entry, and finally synchronously returns `[]string`, the total message count, and the number actually retained. When the total exceeds the limit, the third return value is `messageHistoryMaxSize`; when it does not, the total and retained counts are the same. This output only describes the history that can be retrieved; it is not equivalent to the `logMessages` currently retained in the interactive area.

First, note two points that query consumers will encounter: when a Go rule includes resources, whether the config-generation action can remain in the existing printed output; after changing the configuration for a static sandbox target, whether the final link command changes in a way that can be compared. # Go embed and static linking proposal

Revisiting the initial draft at year-end, I'm keeping the two issues separate in these notes. The resource track is about whether query consumers can trace back to the generation configuration from a single output; the static-linking track is about exactly how the link command changes once the comparison target is fixed. The two tracks can share a single interface review, but results from one should not be used to support the other.

`test/go_rules/single_test.go` is still the known entry point on the test side. The file directly shows only the `package whatever` and `testing` imports. The initial draft treated it as a clue to where resource actions were implemented. That judgment is retained here: we did look in that direction at the time, but no longer use it to determine where the implementation belongs. Files near the tests can only suggest where to find examples to inspect, not which layer assembles the generation action or who passes the static-linking policy to the link stage.

At the time, there were three options on the table for resource representation.

The first was to keep using the existing query print action. Rules with resources and their generation configurations would remain on the same print path, so callers would not need to query regular targets first, then resource objects, and finally guess how the two relate. The trade-off is that once scripts consume the output, action ordering, accompanying text, or diagnostic snippets could all be mistaken for a stable format.

The second was to add a resource-specific action. Resource inputs, generation configurations, and resource-related failures could be surfaced separately, and tests could more easily cover just the resource branch. The problem is not having one more name, but that existing callers would have to recognize a second entry point; if a target requires two queries to reconstruct its generation configuration, troubleshooting would involve extra judgments about how to piece the results together.

The third was to attach resource information as additional fields on regular targets. This looked like the narrowest change, but if the fields describe only the target, readers might not be able to tell where the generation configuration comes from. Resource-related failures could also be mixed into regular target output. This option has not been dropped; it just is not suitable as the default direction at this point.

This round of discussion established only a working preference to "prioritize keeping the existing action that supports tracing back to the configuration." What rules without resources should display, where errors should be reported when resource files cannot be read, and which text in the output can be changed are all still undecided. Without input that includes resources and raw print-output snippets, we cannot turn a conceptual description into a format consumers can already rely on.

The static sandbox comparison has narrower requirements than the resource track. First hold one sandbox target fixed, then save the printed output under the regular and static configurations separately. Before comparing, we must verify that the target, dependencies, and output directory have not been replaced; if they differ, even if an extra option happens to appear in the command, we cannot confirm that the static configuration caused it.

An early quick check was: "Seeing static in the command is enough for a pass." This passage stays because it explains why the initial draft did not give a conclusion outright, but we no longer use it as an assessment method. The presence of a word does not establish that it belongs to the final link stage or that other command conditions did not change at the same time. The static-linking track must at least retain the input target, how the two configurations are distinguished, and command snippets that show the link stage.

There is a similar misreading on the resource side. Finding a test entry point does not establish the shape of the printed fields; seeing the name of a generation action does not establish whether a missing resource file produces an empty result or a failure. Both tracks lack actual inputs and raw outputs, but the gaps differ: the resource track lacks the relationship between the public representation and the generation configuration, while the static-linking track lacks a command comparison for the same target.

If the resource representation prevents existing callers from continuing to trace back through the original action, we should not expand the public surface just to add an entry point. First take the incompatible output snippets and compare the three candidates again. If the additional-fields approach still does not let readers trace back to resource references and the generation configuration, it should not be the default direction either.

If the static-linking comparison also changes the target, dependencies, or output directory, discard that record; do not extract an individual option from it. The material needed for the next round is specific: query output for one Go rule with resources, and the link commands for the same sandbox target under the two configurations, saved side by side.

# Go embed and Static Linking Proposal

This page preserves several different formulations. Initially, it simply recorded together two issues that were likely to come up in printed output; later, someone tried to combine them into a single configuration chain; a subsequent recheck found that resource representation and static linking could share only verification practices, not conclusions. Not all the old paragraphs have been removed, to prevent the same misreading from recurring next time based on a test filename or a single command line.

## 2023-06-26: The Initial Note

The earliest notes were not intended to define all externally visible behavior of Go rules. There was only one narrowly scoped question at the time: if a Go rule with resources needs to generate a configuration, can query consumers still find that step in the existing printed output? The static sandbox was noted alongside it because static configuration also needed to be verified through printed commands, not because a helper shared by the two had already been found.

The repository location recorded at the time was `test/go_rules/single_test.go`. The file header showed `package whatever`, and the file imported `testing`. This provided a place on the test side to put examples and a starting point for subsequent investigation. It did not establish which rule implemented the resource action, much less whether the target rule or a helper assembled the static sandbox's linker arguments.

The note's initial assumption about resources was narrow: hold off on creating a parallel query entry point, and see whether the existing printed output already lets readers trace back to configuration generation. The advantage of this assumption was that it required fewer changes to callers' access paths; its limitation was also recorded from the start—without inputs and outputs containing resources, it was impossible to determine what should be retained in the printed output, or whether related actions would still appear when resources were empty.

The approach on the static-linking side was simpler at the time: take the same sandbox target and inspect the final command once under the normal configuration and once under the static configuration. No actual commands were saved then, so no conclusions were drawn about the options. If the target, dependencies, and output directory all changed together, the comparison would be meaningless; this was already a stopping condition in the initial draft.

## 2023-06-27: Review Margin Notes

The first review did not turn the resource track into a table of fields. The review feedback was to first distinguish "whether callers can trace back to configuration generation" from "whether an action name introduces a separate entry point". The former is a relationship visible to consumers, while the latter is a change to the public surface; they cannot be treated as the same thing simply because both appear around queries.

The review also pointed out that a test file's location cannot stand in for action ownership. This reminder did not completely change the draft at the time, but it repeatedly became a point of correction later: a test file can help organize observations, but it cannot be used to declare that it implements the resource action, nor to determine which layer sandbox Policy Dependencies is in.

There was also only one margin note on the static-linking section: to compare linking results, the subject of comparison must remain fixed. The configuration name alone cannot serve as evidence of success; words such as "static" appearing in a command also do not show that they apply at the final linking stage.

## 2023-12-26: Separating the Candidates

The year-end addendum organized resource representation into three candidates, rather than immediately choosing one as an established interface.

| Candidate | What It Aimed to Preserve at the Time | Cost of Concern at the Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reuse the existing query print action | Callers can trace back to resource references and configuration generation through a single output | Scripts may read the entire printed output, creating implicit burdens around ordering and accompanying text |
| Add a resource-specific action | Resource inputs, generation steps, and resource-related failures can be checked separately | Existing callers must recognize a second entry point and combine two queries |
| Attach it to ordinary target fields | No obvious new action name is added | Readers may not be able to see where the generated configuration comes from, and failure attribution can easily become mixed into ordinary output |

The first option was closest to being ready for a trial at the time. The reason was not that the test path proved anything, but that callers were already accustomed to tracing back from a single printed result. If resource references and configuration generation were split across different entry points, troubleshooting would first require deciding which entry point to query, then deciding whether the two outputs were related.

The second option was not without value. If resource-related failures could be separated from ordinary target failures, tests could focus on covering resource branches, and investigation would be less likely to mistake configuration-generation problems for output problems. But this would place responsibility for choosing the entry point on callers. Neater categorization alone was not enough to offset that compatibility cost.

The third option was retained as a fallback. It appeared to involve smaller changes, but ordinary target fields might not express the relationship between the configuration-generation action and resource references. If readers still had to infer the action's source from field placement, this approach would merely shift the work of interpretation to query consumers.

This version did not decide how to display cases with no resources, nor how failures should appear when resource files could not be read. These were not overlooked polishing details, but areas that should not be treated as settled without inputs and results.

## The Experiment Table Left Blank at the Time

The same addendum also left the following table. The results column was never filled in later, which is more useful than filling it with imagined commands.

| Input | What Needed to Be Inspected | Status at the Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A Go rule with resources | The relationship between resource references and the configuration-generation action in query output | Original output not saved |
| The same sandbox target, normal configuration | The final printed linking command | Original output not saved |
| The same sandbox target, static configuration | Whether an attributable difference appears at the linking stage | Specific input missing |

"The same target" was not a generic reminder. If different targets were used for the normal and static configurations, the target name, dependency set, and output directory could all change together. Even if the commands looked different, the difference could not be attributed to static mode.

The conditions on the resource side were different. The rule had to actually contain resources; the path or test name of `single_test.go` could not stand in for input. The printed result also had to let readers identify the relationship between resource references and the configuration-generation action. Isolated target fields, or an excerpt of generated text without context, would not be enough to answer the original question.

## Quick Judgments Previously Used

The following passage is retained in its old formulation:

> Put resources in additional fields on ordinary targets first; if they cannot be read, have the test entry point run one more scan. A static sandbox can be considered to pass as long as the command contains wording about static linking.

**This passage has been discarded.** The first half treated ordinary fields and generation actions as the same thing, without output showing that they actually corresponded. Even if the test entry point could provide additional observations, it could not prove that a field in an external query was the configuration-generation action. The problem with the second half was more direct: the appearance of a term could not prove that it applied at the linking stage, nor that the target, dependencies, and output directory had remained unchanged.

Another old judgment is also retained: since `test/go_rules/single_test.go` was near the Go rule tests, it could be used to infer where the resource action was implemented. This was later corrected to "test-side location". The `package whatever` and `testing` imports show that the current file is adjacent to tests; they do not identify the resource action, the rule owner, or where arguments are passed to the sandbox helper.

The old approaches can still help locate a starting point for the next recheck, but they can no longer serve as a basis for release decisions. They are retained to explain why this page shifted from "seeing a name" to "saving printed results for the same input".

## 2025-09-05: The Resource Track Returns to Review

PLZ-202 was included in release checks on this date. The card left a to-do to check the Go resource embed action and required that parts without evidence remain blank. It shows that the resource track was still treated as an interface issue to address, not that any particular printed result had already been produced.

This reorganization reaffirmed the boundary of the resource track: it asks only whether inputs containing resources can point to the configuration-generation action in the public query representation. It is not responsible for defining the resource semantics of every kind of Go rule, nor for guaranteeing the static sandbox's linking settings.

At this stage, all three candidates remained viable, but the basis for comparison was clearer. The option that reused the existing action had to let consumers find the relationship between resource references and configuration generation within a single output; the dedicated-action option had to explain how existing callers would recognize the new entry point; the additional-field option had to explain why the fields would not hide the action's source. Without actual excerpts, these remained comparison requirements, not results that had already been achieved.

## 2025-09-12: Addendum After the Review Request

PLZ-202 subsequently moved into review, with the recorded reason that implementation had been completed on an existing branch and was being sent directly to review. This status change could not replace query results showing the resource representation. The existence of an implementation on a branch and what callers could currently read in external printed output were two separate layers of the issue.

The review therefore did not freeze the entire query print output into a fixed format. The more workable direction was to fix only the necessary resource-action indicators and their relationship to configuration generation, without automatically elevating action ordering, explanatory text, and accompanying diagnostics into permanent commitments. If any callers did in fact read a particular ordering or additional text, that would require a separate discussion with actual output; this page has no such caller material.

This addendum also separated the resource and static-linking tracks from a single "configuration issue". The resource side concerned how far the commitments of the public representation should extend; the static-linking side concerned whether investigation should begin with external linking commands or internal policy parameters. The current material contains no call edges for the sandbox helper, so internal parameters cannot be settled in the name of interface review.

## 2025-10-20: The Static-Linking Track Stops Before Inputs

The record for PLZ-219 explicitly states that Static sandbox Link Flag still had one unconfirmed point, specific input was missing, and implementation should not begin yet. This stopping point is retained here to prevent a clearer direction on the resource side from being misread as completion on the static-linking side as well.

The static-linking track should prepare a fixed sandbox target and save one printed result under the normal configuration and one under the static configuration. Before comparing them, first verify that the target, dependencies, and output directory have not changed; only after that prerequisite is met should the differences in the final linking commands be examined. The configuration switch is merely a way to organize this comparison; it cannot by itself prove that the configuration has reached the helper, much less replace the final command.

The early screening method of "seeing the word static is enough" still does not apply here. At most, it is an investigative clue. If the two printed records come from different targets, or one of them changes the dependencies and output directory, the entire comparison should stop, without extracting any individual options from it.

The resource and static-linking tracks remain on the same page because this page preserves the history of that interface review. They do not define a shared implementation boundary: the resource side needs a queryable action representation; the static-linking side still lacks a fixed input and command comparison that can be rechecked.

## Excerpts from the Latest Review

The following two short notes were retained from the review:

> For resource actions, first use print to trace back to configuration generation; do not fill in field names without the original output.

This sentence preserves the working order at the time, but does not specify the text to show when resources are empty, nor answer which error layer applies when resource files fail.

> For the static sandbox, fix the target first, then inspect the final linking command; do not start by tracing the helper.

This sentence identifies external commands as the current observation priority; it does not show that the helper's internal policy parameters have been passed correctly. The latter still requires call edges or saved results before deciding whether to enter another round of discussion.

## Current Position on Resources

After the initial note, the first review, the three candidates, the blank experiment table, the discarded quick judgment, the addenda on two cards, and the pause in the static-linking track, the current requirement is recorded here: a go_library with resources must be queryable and must use embedcfg in the externally visible action representation to identify the generated Go embed configuration.

This requirement fixes the identifier and meaning for rules with resources in the public action representation. Resource verification should use an actual go_library with resources as input and inspect whether query print lets readers identify the action that generates the Go embed configuration. It does not require turning the entire printed output into immutable serialized text; action ordering, accompanying diagnostics, and output portions not described here do not automatically become compatibility commitments because of this sentence.

Likewise, this position does not specify what rules without resources must display, nor which layer should report what kind of error when a resource file cannot be opened. These two issues were identified as gaps early on, and there are still no corresponding inputs and failure results to archive. They should remain part of example verification; conceptual consistency should not replace actual results.

The resource position also does not elevate `test/go_rules/single_test.go` to implementation owner. This file remains an entry point for test observations; resource-action ownership must be established through query output or caller results. Misrepresenting test adjacency as implementation ownership would reintroduce the judgment that has already been discarded.

## Matters Not Yet Split Out

The resource examples need real inputs and query excerpts that preserve the relationship. If no resource action can be found in the result, that should be recorded as an interface discrepancy; if the action exists but readers cannot clearly see its relationship to configuration generation, it must not pass as "close enough" either. Examples without resources can be used to check for false positives, but cannot be used to infer the final text of resource errors.

What the static-linking examples lack is specific input, not more terminology. The two outputs must first let reviewers confirm that the subject of comparison has not been replaced, before they assess differences at the linking stage. If the record contains only configuration names or a single excerpted line, the next attempt should still restart from the full commands.

An adjacent issue that has not yet been split onto its own page is whether callers depend on the ordering or accompanying diagnostics of the entire query print output. All that is currently known is that this may create a compatibility burden; there is no material showing what specific callers read, so this page does not expand the commitments of the resource representation.

## Appendix of Old Examples

The following two old examples remain on record.

> If there are no resource results, leave it blank.

This statement can explain the early reluctance to fill in fields based on test paths, but it does not distinguish between no resources, an action not appearing, and an action failing, and cannot replace the current position on resources.

> If the command differs in static mode, record static linking as passing for now.

This example no longer applies. Without a fixed target, dependency set, and output directory, a command difference has no value for attribution. It is retained here only to show that the misjudgment at the time arose from insufficient comparison conditions, not that the resource track had already supplied evidence for the static-linking track.

# Test entry point and sandbox troubleshooting tree

## Same starting point, narrower meaning

At first, the issue name and call name kept leading the search for the test main program generation entry point to `tools/please_go_test/gotest/test_data/main/example_test_main.go`. The old path is still a useful place to start a recheck: it is under the test data directory, and `package parse` and `import (` are visible in the file header. But the initial record made "we can find the file" sound too much like "we found the generation entry point," making it easy for later readers of this page to treat them as the same thing.

This recheck starts with only what the file itself can establish. If it can be opened, that confirms a sample source file, its package, and its direct imports. If it cannot be opened, that confirms that its location in the old revision needs to be found again. Neither outcome establishes the generation action, its inputs, where the file is written, or how it is used at runtime.

The earlier approach still has some value. For an issue with the same name, starting from this path is still reasonable, because it is the only local anchor consistently retained in the old material. What has changed is the stopping point: after reading the sample file, no longer treat the directory name, filename, or `package parse` as evidence of a generation relationship.

## Sketch left by the on-call

The original on-call note was short; it was later expanded into the branches below. There is no need to trace the entire chain in one pass, only to keep the two types of symptoms separate at the outset.

```text
Test main program side
|
+- Only have example_test_main.go
|  |
|  +- File is readable: record path, package, imports
|  |                   Then look for the name or result of the generation action
|  |
|  `- File is unreadable: check whether the old path still exists
|                        Don't immediately classify this as a generation failure
|
+- Have a suspected generation action
|  |
|  +- No inputs or write location: keep the name; leave pending investigation
|  |
|  `- Have a resulting file: compare the result with the sample to see if they are the same object
|
`- Only have a secondhand account
   `- Note which side the account came from; don't infer who created it
```

"Compare the result with the sample" asks just one narrow question: is the file in front of us an input sample for the action, or a result written by it? If that cannot be answered, the file should not be labeled as an output in the record. Someone previously tried to infer a write relationship from the two terms `main` and `test_data`, but the recheck found nothing to support that inference.

## Retracted shortcuts

One review reduced the issue to "The file is in `example_test_main.go`, so it is the implementation entry point for the test main program generator." That statement is now marked **discarded**. The path did exist; the mistake was turning an accessible location into a claim about where the implementation lives.

Another inference came up in the same round: sandbox Policy Dependencies and the test entry point were mentioned together, so they must share inputs. The source material had no policy inputs, call sites, return contents, or error output to support that claim, so it was retracted as well. Two symptoms can be reported at the same time; that does not automatically mean they share a source.

Retracting these claims does not require removing the old path from the page. The old issue will still bring readers here; deleting the path would only send people back to guessing from the filename. Keep the path, with a note next to it: use it to look up the sample's location again, not to determine the generation action or sandbox policy.

## Handle sandbox separately

The sandbox side initially had only the words "policy dependency issue." Without independent output, it should remain a symptom that has not been broken down, rather than becoming the last step in the test main program branch. The following branches were added later:

```text
sandbox Policy Dependencies issue
|
+- Have policy input and a return value or error
|  `- Retain the inputs and results in the order they appeared
|
+- Only have an error fragment
|  `- Record where the error appeared; don't infer the policy from the test sample
|
+- Only have a name or a one-line secondhand account
|  `- Go back to the entry point that produced the account and look for the original content
|
`- No independent result
   `- Leave unconfirmed; don't fold it into the test entry-point branch
```

Here, an "independent result" means content that can clearly be attributed to sandbox. A piece of file text seen after the test main program has been generated does not automatically become a sandbox return value. Conversely, seeing only a policy error is not grounds for writing that the test main program has already been generated. With the branches split, one side of the investigation can be completed first without waiting for the other side to round out a conclusion.

## Where the recheck stopped

This recheck still only confirmed the test data path and file header. No actual write location was recorded, and no runtime result was retained that could link the sample to a generation action. The test main program side therefore stopped at "sample located; generation relationship unconfirmed."

No inputs or return values were added on the sandbox side either. The old note says "don't guess the policy from the directory name." That still applies; it is not a complete procedure, just a guard against mistaking the location of a file under `tools` for the source of the policy.

The review's margin notes call for preserving two stopping points: when the sample is readable but no generation action can be found, do not add further explanations to the file; when a policy issue is known only by name, do not use the sample file to fill in a cause. This leaves gaps, but is easier to recheck than joining two gaps into a seemingly complete story.

## Questions still in the margin

The existing record does not answer whether the generated test main program is always written back to `example_test_main.go`. If a result file becomes available later, check where it was written first, then decide whether it is related to this sample.

Another question is whether the sandbox helper's policy dependency could affect the generated file. No call stack or output that could establish the relationship was saved here. The two questions remain on the same page so that people arriving from the old issue name can see that they once appeared side by side, not to merge them again.

# Test Entry Point and sandbox Troubleshooting Tree

## 2023-06-05: The File Location First Recorded

This page did not begin with a complete incident record, but with a path that kept coming up: `tools/please_go_test/gotest/test_data/main/example_test_main.go`. With both "test main program generation" and "sandbox Policy Dependencies" in the issue title at the time, the investigation needed a location that could be opened, so that path was recorded as the entry point.

Opening it revealed only the file header:

```text
package parse
import (
```

The initial record used these two lines as the basis for the next step: first record the package and direct import statements, then look outward using names such as `tools`, `please_go`, and test main program generation. The file itself was under a test data path, making it a suitable observation point on the sample side. That record did not preserve the name of the generation action, did not state what input the action accepted, and did not explain where the result would be written.

A very short working rule was also left at the time: when the sample is readable, do not adjust generation parameters in the sample; when the sample cannot be read, first check whether this location still exists in the old revision. This rule addressed the order of the initial steps. It did not, and should not be read to, mean "the sample file is responsible for generation."

sandbox Policy Dependencies was written in the margin of the same page. The initial wording did not distinguish between "reported at the same time" and "having the same source." No policy input, response content, error excerpt, or call location was preserved, so at the time it could only be listed as a parallel observation.

The old note included this sentence: **Finding the file means finding the entry point.**

The original sentence is retained here because many older issues use this wording to point readers back to the path. In its original context, it meant "there is a place Fang Ke to start investigating," not "the generator has been found." It was precisely this overcompressed phrasing that later led the directory location to carry a conclusion it could not support.

## On-Call Margin Notes for 2023-06

The early note was incomplete, with only two sets of branches:

```text
Can example_test_main.go be opened?
  Yes: first record package/import, then look outward for the generation action.
  No: verify the old path; do not immediately report a generator failure.

Does sandbox have a separate result?
  Yes: record it separately.
  No: do not infer the policy from the directory name.
```

The value of this note was that it separated the file location from runtime observations. It did not require a complete call chain during on-call work, nor did it treat a filename as an action name. As long as what was visible was sample source code, the record could stop on the sample side; as long as sandbox had no result of its own, the record could stop on the policy side.

The note also had obvious gaps. It did not explain which public object to look for first when "looking outward," did not explain how to identify whether a name referred to an actual action, and did not explain how to distinguish an input sample from a written result. Later, someone filled these gaps with assumptions, creating the next layer of misinterpretation.

## 2024-03-18: Mistakenly Combining the Two During a Recheck

When the same path was opened again, the file was still read as a sample in the test data, and its header still began with `package parse`. No newly generated file was saved during the recheck, and no input/output record was obtained that could connect the sample to the action that created it. The conclusion should therefore have stopped at "the sample location can still be revisited."

But a convenient shortcut was proposed at the time: since the issue was at `example_test_main.go`, this file must be the implementation entry point for the test main program generator; since sandbox Policy Dependencies was also listed alongside the same issue, they must share a single chain.

This judgment is now marked **obsolete**. It was withdrawn not because the path later disappeared, but because the path had only ever indicated the file's location. The filename, the `test_data` directory, `package parse`, and the visible import statements cannot establish what writes the file; nor can they establish where the sandbox policy gets its dependencies.

The mistaken judgment was not deleted at the time, and the reason for withdrawing it was left alongside it instead. Older issues often still lead in through the same names; if only the current wording remained, later readers would not know why the page repeatedly emphasizes "the sample is not the implementation." Retaining the incorrect judgment shows that this restriction reflects an actual misreading that occurred here, rather than abstract caution.

## An Unsuccessful Attempt to Fill the Gaps

After the recheck, an attempt was made to expand the old note into a fixed set of generation steps. This attempt was not completed. The existing material contains no commands actually used by those steps, no verifiable write location, and no corresponding runtime output. Turning it into a complete operating procedure would make the page read more smoothly, but would present information that had not been obtained as established fact.

What was retained was therefore not a set of assumed commands, but a narrower decision sequence: first identify what you have in hand.

```text
Only a sample file is available
  -> Record the path, package, and import
  -> Look for the object serving as the generation entry point; if none is found, stop at locating the sample

Only a generation-related name is available
  -> Retain the name
  -> Without input or a write location, do not mark it as having created the sample

File contents and a write location are available
  -> Then ask whether the file is an input sample or the result of an action

Only a secondhand account of the issue is available
  -> First return to the object the account refers to, without filling in call relationships
```

"Then ask" here does not require comparing two files line by line. It only requires answering one local question: is the content in front of you a sample that existed before the action, or a result produced after this action. The generation branch can proceed only when that question can be answered; when it cannot, leave the missing write information unresolved at that point.

This also explains why the old path was not discarded. It remains a local anchor in the old material that can be reopened, suitable for checking the sample's presence. The only change is that the path is no longer the endpoint for attributing cause. The earlier problem was mistakenly writing "implemented here" instead of "start looking here."

## The sandbox Branch Was Not Resolved Along with the File Branch

sandbox Policy Dependencies has always lacked runtime material of its own in the original notes. Placing it alongside the test main program heading only establishes that the two terms appeared in the same investigation context; it does not establish that the test sample supplied input to sandbox, still less that policy dependencies affected the sample file.

Later versions of the page therefore listed sandbox as a separate branch:

```text
sandbox Policy Dependencies anomaly
|
+- Policy input and an independent response are available
|  `- Preserve the order in which the input, response, or error appeared
|
+- An error excerpt is available, but no input
|  `- Record the stage where the error occurred; do not use the test sample to fill in the policy source
|
+- Only a secondhand report of a "dependency anomaly"
|  `- Return to the entry point that produced the report and find the original result
|
`- No independent result
   `- Keep it unconfirmed, without merging it into the test main program conclusion
```

An independent response means content that can be assigned separately to the sandbox branch. File text appearing on the test main program side is not a policy response, even if it was seen during the same period as the issue. Conversely, a policy error excerpt with no trace of test main program generation cannot be used to infer that generation has already occurred.

This branch looks cumbersome on the old page because it does not quickly produce a common cause. It is retained to prevent "appeared at the same time" from being written as "caused one another" again next time. If material was collected for only one side during the investigation, the other side can remain blank; the gaps on the two sides cannot fill one another.

## Review Excerpts for 2024-03

The review did not call for deleting the old path, nor did it accept "the filename is the generation entry point." The comments left can be summarized in two points: the sample path can serve as an anchor for revisiting the issue; opening the sample only locates the file, it does not confirm the generation relationship.

The review also required explicit stopping conditions. The previous version made it easy to keep guessing along the directory hierarchy, eventually producing an explanation unsupported by runtime material. Subsequent records used the following stopping points:

- When the file is readable but the generation entry-point object or write location has not been obtained, stop at locating the sample.
- When a generation-related name is found but there is no input/output relationship, stop at confirming the name.
- When all that remains for sandbox is a name, a screenshot description, or a single secondhand statement, stop at recording the observation.
- When both sides are mentioned but separate results cannot be obtained, retain them as parallel observations.

These stopping points do not declare the issue closed. They only define boundaries this page must not cross. Further investigation should start with the missing object, input, write location, response content, or error location, rather than reinterpreting the package name or directory name already seen.

## 2024-07: Why the Old Approach Is Still Retained

Someone suggested rewriting all the early text in current terms, especially replacing every occurrence of "entry point." This was not done. Older issues still reference this page, and readers may see the old path and old note first; if the page retained only the final wording, it would instead obscure why earlier investigations reached the sample file.

The old approach is therefore retained, but its role is reduced:

```text
Old approach: first open example_test_main.go
Can still be used to: confirm the old sample location and file header
Cannot now be used to: identify the generation action, establish the write relationship, or identify the source of the sandbox policy
```

The second and third lines here place local restrictions on the old approach, rather than denying the path's value. If the file is unreadable in the old revision, locating the file takes priority; unreadability does not automatically mean the generator is broken, still less that it is a sandbox anomaly.

If the file is readable but yields only `package parse` and import statements, that also only establishes that the sample-side observation still holds. You can continue looking outward at this point, but until there is a new generation object, package path, or write location, the sample should not be relabeled as a result file.

## What Each of the Two Lines of Investigation Needs

On the test main program side, the minimum usable record is not a complete source walkthrough, but a distinction between three kinds of material: the sample file, the object serving as the generation entry point, and the written result of an action. All three may appear in the same issue, or only one may be obtained. The file location can stand in for only the first kind, not the latter two.

The minimum record on the sandbox side is likewise not a vague statement that "there is a problem with the policy," but a distinction between whether policy input has been obtained, whether response content exists, and whether an error excerpt exists. If only one item is obtained, retaining that item and where it appeared is enough. Without input, do not infer its input from the test main program's sample path; without a response, do not treat the generated file as the response either.

After breaking the material into these small items, you may sometimes find that the same investigation simply does not contain enough information to answer "are the two related." This is not a troubleshooting failure. Explicitly documenting the material that was not obtained is closer to what actually happened than combining a directory, a filename, and a secondhand statement into a definite causal relationship.

## 2025-09-03: Rechecking from the Public Entry Point

The latest revisit did not rewrite the earlier path, but narrowed the generation branch's search to the public helper. First confirm whether the object being examined is a public build target, then confirm the subcommands it provides, and only then check the package import path required by the generation action and the actual write location. This avoids guessing commands backward from a sample file, while giving "input" and "result" separate places to be recorded.

The current requirements for the test main program generation entry point are as follows: the public target //tools/please_go:please_go provides the testmain subcommand; the caller uses --import_path to pass the package import path and --output to specify the write location for the generated test main program.

This requirement covers only the test main program generation branch. After confirming the public target, do not immediately backfill the sample file; after confirming the subcommand, do not assume the write location just because the package import path has appeared. The two items must be checked separately. If only one is obtained, the record should remain marked as incomplete.

Here, the sample path serves as a reference for later comparison. If the write location of an actual result does fall at `tools/please_go_test/gotest/test_data/main/example_test_main.go`, that action and the sample record can be included in the same recheck entry; if the locations differ, the old path remains only an entry point to the old sample. Without a write location, the file contents cannot be marked as the result generated by that action.

This requirement also does not change the sandbox branch's stopping points. The public helper's generation entry point belongs to the test main program side and cannot substitute for policy input, a policy response, or a sandbox error location. Even if the two things appear in the same investigation context again, first preserve the local content of each separately.

## Minimum Content When Documenting a Recheck

On the file side, you can record only: whether `tools/please_go_test/gotest/test_data/main/example_test_main.go` was opened, whether `package parse` is still visible, and whether there are direct import statements. If these are all that were confirmed this time, stopping the record here is sufficient, without inventing a generation relationship.

On the generation side, you can record only: whether what was found is a public target, a subcommand, a package import path, or a write location. These are not the same level of information. Without a write location, no sample file should be described as output; without a package import path, a name cannot be expanded into a usable invocation either.

On the sandbox side, you can record only: whether there is independent input, response content, or an error excerpt. If none of the three exists, simply write "no independent result obtained." A common earlier misreading was that the troubleshooting page must provide conclusions about both the test entry point and policy dependencies; the old investigation did not provide such complete material.

## Issues Not Yet Split Out

The existing material does not preserve the process by which the generated test main program enters the subsequent execution stage. Neither `package parse` nor the sample path answers this question. If a generation result is obtained later, first record the write location and result file, then decide whether to continue investigating the execution stage.

There is likewise no existing input, response, or call stack for determining whether the sandbox helper's policy dependencies change the generated file. If the two observations appear together in the future, still preserve them under the two branches first; appearing at the same time is not evidence of a connection.

This page also does not confirm whether the test data layout in the old revision matches the later layout. The fact that the path can still be navigated only establishes that the starting point of the old record remains identifiable, not that the file contents, write relationship, or policy dependencies are unchanged.

## Retained Appendix from the Old Meeting

The earliest meeting shorthand is still appended at the end:

```text
Entry point = file? Undetermined.
sandbox = appeared at the same time, but no response was obtained.
First record parse/import.
Do not change the implementation based on the example name.
```

These lines contain no parameters, no write location, and no indication of which action is responsible for generating the file, so they cannot be treated as current operational conclusions. What they preserve is the boundary of the investigation at the time: the file could be opened, but the generation relationship was undetermined; sandbox was mentioned, but no independent response was obtained.

There is also an old annotation alongside the appendix saying "finding the file counts as finding the entry point." This sentence is obsolete. When reopening the old page, a readable file only means that you can continue looking outward; it does not mean that the test main program generation relationship has been fully checked, nor that there is already an answer for sandbox Policy Dependencies.

# Resource References and Remote Input Decision Record

This record originally put two names on the same line: Resource Reference Serialization, Remote shell Input Download Sequence. Both were included in the history of the "compatibility train", and only later did it become clear that grouping them together did not mean they shared an implementation point. The old draft still retains this combined framing because it accurately reflects the initial search perspective; the notes below only append the reviews and trade-offs that have already taken place, rather than rewriting the earlier judgment as though it never existed.

## The Path Left by the Initial Draft

The first file the search led to was `src/query/print.go`. The visible local information was `package query` and `import (`; the index describes it as an existing go module for code reading and checking historical behavior. The old record used query, print, and `res` as search terms, so it treated this file as the common entry point for both requirements. This identification was useful for "where to start looking", but did not sufficiently support "what performs the entire action".

The working hypothesis recorded at the time was: resource reference serialization first goes through the externally visible representation of query print, and the download order for remote shell input might also be reflected downstream of that same output relationship. No specific calls, arguments, generated files, or failure text were retained, so this statement has remained only the old framing. The initial draft's decision was not to split the page for the time being, but first to add the visible results of one success and one failure. There was no card to cite at the time, and the page did not present these two results as verified facts.

## Following Up on the Resource Item First

The follow-up review of resource references was later tracked under PLZ-206. Its initial requirement was simply to retain the visible results of "Resource Reference Serialization" from one successful call and one failed call separately. Work began on the morning of day 23 of month 9 and was marked complete that afternoon; the action log shows that the work moved from To Do to In Progress and then to Done, but these actions themselves did not include success output, failure output, or the original text of either.

Therefore, "completed" cannot stand in for "results archived". This page can confirm that the review took place, but it cannot reconstruct the specific content printed by query print from status changes, nor can it attribute a particular output format to the implementation not shown in `src/query/print.go`. The historical decision on the resource item was revised to have two layers: retain the old draft's statement about the search entry point, while leaving the missing success/failure samples as a documentation gap. A single completed status cannot erase that gap.

This also changes how strongly the original combined judgment can be stated. Resource Reference Serialization remains a topic on this page, but it is no longer described as a prerequisite step in the remote download sequence. The two tracks share only historical context and one search entry point, not an unverified causal relationship.

## The Separate Record for Remote Input

Remote shell Input Download Sequence corresponds to PLZ-223. The requirement recorded on the card is fairly specific: rerun the corresponding entry point on platforms supported by the maintainers, and check the files actually generated and their versions. The historical action on day 22 of month 10 marked this case as `failure_classified`. This shows that the failure had already been classified, but provides no category name, runtime platform, generated filename, or version value.

A distinction that the old draft could easily obscure is retained here: the resource review focuses on externally visible results during a call; the remote input review focuses on what remains after the entry point runs, and whether the files and versions match. The former's "printed out" cannot prove the latter's "download completed", and the latter's failure classification cannot be used to infer the resource serialization format. The current material does not contain enough detail to determine whether the download occurs before or after shell input parsing, or is performed by another adjacent action. This timing question remains unresolved on this page, rather than being a conclusion that can be casually filled in from a filename.

## Three Approaches That Were Debated

The first approach was to continue treating `src/query/print.go` as the shared implementation location. It required the least effort and was closest to the old investigation record, but would misread "search hit" as "the action is completed here". It would also make the output checks in PLZ-206 and the platform reruns in PLZ-223 look like the same test, which the actual material does not state.

The second approach was to treat the path only as a search entry point, with resources and remote input each retaining their own observations. This preserves the original record's value for finding information without inventing a story for call edges that were not recorded. The cost is that readers cannot obtain the complete sequence from the filename alone; confirming the sequence still requires returning to the actual rerun records for the corresponding entry point.

The third approach was to split this into two pages immediately, one covering only resources and the other only remote shell. This would give the cleanest boundaries, but would lose the context of why they were recorded together in the same round of compatibility work, and would make the old draft's mistaken combined judgment harder to trace. The existing material does not require deleting the old page, nor does it provide two sets of results sufficient for standalone pages.

The decision in this round is to use the second approach, without deleting traces of the first approach from the old paragraphs. `src/query/print.go` is retained as a starting point for follow-up checks; this page no longer attributes both actions to it. Resource Reference Serialization and Remote shell Input Download Sequence are discussed separately in the main text, each using only observations that have been retained. If the page is split later, the trigger will be that both sides have their own success/failure records or generated-file records, not merely that the title contains two slash-separated topics.

## Misreadings Left Along the Way

The term "common entry point" in the old draft actually mixed three things: the search terms matched the file, the file belongs to the query package, and the output might be related to resource markers. The first is recorded, the second is visible in the file header, and the third was only the interpretation at the time. They cannot be combined into an implementation chain. The old wording is still retained because documenting the history of the requirements is one of this page's purposes; however, when "entry point" is used in the subsequent text, it means the starting point for searching and checking, not proof that a remote download was completed.

Likewise, the term remote shell cannot stand in for the specific object involved. The current material confirms only that "input download timing" is something to check during the call. Without shell commands, a platform list, filenames, version numbers, or request logs, `failure_classified` cannot be interpreted as a network failure, a permission failure, or a generation failure. A failure classification exists, but the classification details are still blank.

## The Retained State Diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CombinedRecord
    CombinedRecord --> PathRecheck: Match for query/print
    PathRecheck --> TwoObservations: Resource results and remote timing kept separate
    TwoObservations --> ResourceSamplesMissing: PLZ-206 status completed
    TwoObservations --> RemoteEntryPointReviewPending: PLZ-223 failure classified
    ResourceSamplesMissing --> [*]
    RemoteEntryPointReviewPending --> [*]
```

"Completed" in the diagram indicates only the historical action status, not that this page obtained the original output text; "failure classified" likewise indicates only the status recorded on the card, not that the cause of failure is known. These statuses are retained to distinguish what was done from what evidence was left behind.

## The Decisions Ultimately Settled On

This page will continue to be retained as a long-term reference, but the scope of its decisions has narrowed. Decision one: `src/query/print.go`, found during the old investigation, can serve as a starting point for searches and code reading. Decision two: the full implementation of Resource Reference Serialization cannot be attributed to this path alone. Decision three: Remote shell Input Download Sequence must be considered separately, based on entry point reruns on supported platforms, the files actually generated, and version checks; for now, this page records only that requirement and one failure classification, not results that do not exist.

These three decisions do not establish the final compatibility position for 2026.09. They only define how this page preserves the changes in understanding that have already occurred: the early combined judgment remains above, the resource review status from month 9 remains in the resource section, the remote failure classification from month 10 remains in the remote section, and the path can still be revisited but is no longer used to explain more than the material supports. Readers searching only for `query` or `print` can still find this page; once they open it, they need to read the path hit, output review, and download timing separately.

## Appendix of Earlier Examples

**Earlier Example One: Treating a File Hit as Implementation Attribution.**

The initial draft can be read as "query print found → two requirements related → awaiting verification through one call". This wording did not fabricate results, but made a common entry point sound too much like a shared implementation. It is retained as a historical example, but no longer applies.

**Earlier Example Two: Treating a Completed Status as a Complete Set of Samples.**

The resource review on PLZ-206 had already moved from In Progress to Done, and that status can still be used to show the action timeline. It cannot replace success output and failure output; the original samples were not included in this record. The same boundary applies to `failure_classified` for the remote item: the classification status is retained, but the specific category is not filled in. Both earlier examples are placed in the appendix to prevent later readers from treating them as current conclusions.

Finally, one TODO remains: after the raw results for both entry points have been added, decide whether to split the page and whether the historical relationship between "resource references" and "remote shell" needs to be rewritten.

# Proposal for Updating the Module Download Diagram

This draft retains a diagram trial from the cumulative compatibility train; it is not a current description of the module download process. The initial draft focused on the node ordering of download-only Update Graph; only during a later review did we find that the part of the diagram easiest to misread was not the download node itself, but the unstated states on either side of it. People still use the old diagram to find the entry point, so it was not deleted; the constraints that applied at the time are added here.

The original idea was simple: start from the state before the call, pass through the module download action, and then inspect the final discovery list. The benefit of drawing it this way is that readers can distinguish between "download complete" and "the list has been generated." That is also where the problem lies. If a trace retains only the final list, the line still looks complete, but there is no evidence showing at which stage the list changed. The initial draft treated this gap as a detail to fill in; it should now be treated as a condition for determining whether a line can be drawn.

`test/go_rules/single_test.go` is the local pointer left by the earlier investigation. The file header shows `package whatever` and `import "testing"`, indicating that it is an entry point for inspecting a test file. It does not identify ownership of the module download action or provide the implementation path for download-only. Previously recording the issue name, call name, and this file side by side made it easy to assume that the three formed a call relationship; that inference is no longer used. The path can still be used to revisit the testing context at the time, but it should not be included in the scope of responsibility of the updated diagram.

The PLZ-207 pair later went through interface review. That review only shows that "Module Download Sequence" was reviewed as interface-level material; it cannot replace a rerun record containing both before and after states. The change left after the review was to split the observation targets: the state before the call, the rule-file location, the position adjacent to the download action, and the final discovery list. These are not fields that must all be present every time; when one is missing, the diagram must stop at the positions already available rather than using another trace to fill the gap and create one continuous line.

There were originally three candidate ways to draw it.

**A: Annotate the old diagram.** Keep the download action in place, and mark the "state on entry" and the "list read location" before and after the action. A is closest to the initial draft and suits old records that already have the nodes but lack explanation. The cost is that adjacent actions may still be read as the same phase; if the download completion point and the list read point remain indistinguishable after annotation, A has not resolved the original ambiguity.

**B: Make download-only a standalone segment.** The left endpoint of this segment is limited to the state before that call, and the right endpoint to the final discovery list in the same record, with the download action in the middle. B makes the diagram boundaries clearer and also makes it easier to replace the entry-point name in the diagram later. The cost is that it requires more evidence: if the rule-file location cannot be revisited, or if the two endpoints come from different traces, they cannot be connected into the same segment. B was the approach favored at the time, not a migration decision that had already been implemented.

**C: Retain only the download node.** This requires the least maintenance and does not draw any unseen states, but it cannot answer whether completion left any additional visible change. The initial draft briefly treated C as the safe default diagram; after review, it was not retained because it hides the before-and-after relationship that actually needs to be checked. C can still be used for old records where only the action name is known, but it cannot serve as a conclusion about ordering.

The PLZ-224 pair offers another way to look at it: find a repository trace that still depends on download-only Update Graph, and record the rule-file location and final discovery list. This entry point is closer to the existing user path than a diagram alone, but it likewise cannot establish that all modules share one action order. If a trace provides only the rule file and the list, it can at most validate the right side of the diagram; if it provides only the state before the call, it can at most confirm the left side. When the two endpoints do not appear in the same record, do not fill in the intermediate causality.

During review, lay the materials out and read them in order of occurrence rather than comparing node names first. First check what is visible before the call begins, then at which location the rule file was confirmed, and finally the discovery list after completion. If the download action appears only in the issue description and has no adjacent state, mark it as mentioned rather than located. This does not make the diagram more complete, but it prevents turning "a download exists" into "the order has been proven."

The old draft also left behind an overly strong assertion: as long as the two final discovery lists are the same, the same update diagram can continue to be used. That no longer applies. Identical lists may simply mean that neither record retained the intermediate changes; conversely, different lists cannot be directly attributed to the download action. The diagram can express only the adjacent relationships actually retained; it cannot replace a judgment about the source of the difference.

No long-term choice is being made between A and B at this point. If the annotations on the old diagram are sufficient for readers to distinguish the state before the call, the download completion point, and the list read point, continue using A; if the three positions are still collapsed into one node on the diagram, use B instead. When switching, change only how the diagram is expressed; do not replace the rule file, input conditions, and discovery list along with it. Otherwise, even if the diagram becomes clearer, it will not be possible to tell where the difference came from.

The withdrawal conditions remain as in the initial draft, but the interpretation is narrower: withdraw newly added connecting lines when the state before the call is missing, the rule-file location cannot be revisited, the same record has no final discovery list, or the order can only be inferred from the issue name. Withdrawing them does not negate the module download action; it only means that this material is insufficient to support the ordering shown in the diagram. Keep the old diagram, the visible rule-file location, and the unconfirmed items on file, and decide whether to redraw once a trace with complete before-and-after evidence appears.

```text
Obtain a failure record or a record awaiting completion
```
