The work item associated with PLZ-225 requires triggering the corresponding job through an existing automation entry point in the repository and recording the job, commit, and actual artifact name. The three items must point to the same execution run. The job is used to locate the execution itself, the commit confirms the code it corresponds to, and the actual artifact name rules out mixing together outputs of the same type. If all you have is a failure status and none of these three items, do not open a failure log that merely looks similar.

Only after the job identity is complete should you collect the failed command and exit code. The failed command identifies which step exited, while the exit code tells you what the command returned on this run. Both must come from the same job: if the command is copied from job A and the exit code from job B, they cannot be saved as one context even if the failure text is exactly the same.

Sometimes only a summary failure status is visible. You may retain the status, but record the command context as empty; do not turn "job failed" into "Git command failed". Conversely, if you have the failed command but no exit code, save the command and mark the exit code as missing; do not fill it in with the exit code from another job of the same type. Inspect the output before and after the command only when it can be matched to that job, commit, and artifact.

When the command context is still missing, troubleshooting stops at "failure result seen, command not retrieved". At that point, you cannot determine whether the exit occurred during parameter handling, in Git itself, or during subsequent archiving. Also, do not assign the two items to the same recovery action merely because the single-label track also contains a failed unit.

## Save Same-Run Comparisons for Single-Label Runs

The local entry point for PLZ-208 is to run "Single-Tag Tool Parameters" through the existing test entry point and record the affected unit and adjacent unchanged unit. At the start of the run, first record the actual label passed in and the location at which the entry point receives it; at the end of the run, record the raw output for each of the two unit groups. The adjacent unchanged unit is the same-run control, not a substitute for the affected unit, and it cannot be used to prove that the Git subprocess is normal.

There are three common stopping conditions.

1. The test entry point did not start, or after starting it did not reach parameter handling. Copy the entry-side symptom into the record verbatim and stop here. Do not rewrite a startup failure as "the single label was rejected", because no parameter-handling action has been observed.
2. The affected unit has output, but the adjacent unchanged unit has no result from the same run. The existing output can be archived; do not perform the comparison yet. Any control added later must state that it belongs to the same run; even if the target name is the same, a result from another run cannot be added as the neighbor.
3. Both unit groups have output, but the actual label was not saved. The results are still useful, but you cannot infer the label value or parameter form from the output. Keep the input gap in the record; do not guess from the result.

The input, entry location, and output should all be in the same run material. Temporarily switching the test target, switching the command, or pasting output from another run into the current record can serve only as material for another investigation, not to fill this sample. If the failure occurred before parameter handling, still save the failure text as an entry-side symptom; do not reduce it to an abstract conclusion detached from the entry point.

At minimum, the single-label side must show: the actual label, the affected unit, the adjacent unchanged unit, the two sets of output, and whether parameter handling was reached. If any item is missing, record the items already present and stop at the corresponding point. A standalone green output from one affected unit cannot offset the absence of another unit; the output from one neighbor cannot show that the label did not affect other paths.

## Old Paths Are Only Lookup Entry Points

Old issue names and call names direct inspection to `tools/please_pex/pex_main.py`. The direct dependencies in that file header include `from importlib import import_module`, `from zipfile import ZipFile, ZipInfo, is_zipfile`, `import os`, and `import runpy`. These adjacent references can help decide whether to inspect module loading, ZIP checks, or nearby archive reads first, but the path itself does not provide the failure location for any given run.

The presence of `is_zipfile` or `ZipFile` in a file does not mean that the single-label parameter necessarily passes through archiving; `import_module` and `runpy` likewise do not by themselves explain why a Git command failed. Only when the current run material traces the failed command to these adjacent references should you continue tracing back through the same job or test. Without such a connection, the path serves only as a lookup entry left by an old record.

After reading the PEX path, first cross-check it against the current sample: do the test entry, label input, job, or failed command belong to the run being recorded? If there is only a path and no input or command context, do not choose a recovery method based on the filename. If there is a path and a failed command, but the job, commit, or actual artifact name cannot be aligned, still stop on the job-identity side; the path cannot replace job identity.

## How to Close Out the Two Records

The final single-label record should allow review of the test entry point, actual label, affected unit, adjacent unchanged unit, and both sets of output. If the entry did not reach parameter handling, retaining the entry-side symptom is sufficient. The Git record should allow review of the automation entry point, job, commit, actual artifact name, failed command, and exit code; leave missing items missing, and do not fill them in from another run. Attach the PEX path only if the investigation actually passed through it, and state whether it is on the same chain as the failed command.

PLZ-208 are used to locate single-label run materials, and PLZ-225 are used to locate Git job materials. They belong to the same compatibility train, but they do not share inputs, outputs, or recovery actions. DOC-22 are another set of compatibility-check objects; here, retain only the navigation relationship and do not bring the verification content of Remote Request SDK And metadata into this troubleshooting tree.

At handoff, ask three specific questions first: Did the single-label value and the two sets of output come from the same run? Do Git's job, commit, and actual artifact name correspond to one another? Did the failed command and exit code come from that run? If any answer is no, leave the record in the corresponding branch. A record left as "only the entry-side symptom", "only the failure status", or "command not retrieved" is not a complete conclusion, but it is more reliable than combining different situations into a single causal chain.

# Remote Requests and Go Dependency Integration Workflow

This round keeps separate records for two items in the same release train: whether request metadata can still reach the action through the existing entry point after the remote-request SDK upgrade; and how Go dependencies should remain classified between the regular build and test entry points. Both may manifest as changes in results, but their inputs, reproduction entry points, and recovery methods differ, so the output from one section cannot replace the records for the other.

The remote-request review still starts with `src/remote/action.go`. This file is in the `remote` package, and what is currently visible is the direct import block at the top of the file. This can serve as a navigation point near the request action, starting with locating call sites and existing automation entry points; the fact that the issue title once pointed to this file does not justify attributing all metadata changes to the action itself. The observation of a result regression after the Remote Request SDK And metadata upgrade corresponds to work item PLZ-209.

Before starting the review, use a pre-migration invocation that is still available as the baseline. Save the input, the entry point that triggered it, and the actual artifact name. The post-upgrade invocation must use the same entry point. PLZ-209 requires retaining the job, commit, and actual artifact name; these three items are not intended to label the result, but to let others determine whether the two outputs came from the same automation path. Keeping only a failure message makes it impossible to tell whether it is a reproduction after the SDK adjustment or a temporary attempt on a different commit.

The decision sequence for the remote-request section is as follows.

1. First compare the request bodies. If the inputs differ, return to the call adaptation code first, rather than inferring a metadata problem from the action's result.
2. If the request bodies are the same, record the request metadata visible before and after the action. Record only where the differences appear, without assuming that either SDK or the action has exclusive ownership of the metadata.
3. Continue investigating around the remote action only if the metadata is the same but the actual artifacts differ; if the artifacts are the same but the metadata differs, retain this as a compatibility observation, and do not document it as having already caused a regression.
4. If there is no baseline record using the same input, leave the status unconfirmed. Do not directly describe a single result as a remote service failure, and do not adjust Go dependencies on that basis.

The old notes attributed the "result regression" directly to the remote action. That was an investigative lead from the initial triage, and it remains here as a starting point for review, but no longer serves as a migration conclusion. Requests after the SDK upgrade, information added by the caller, and behavior around the action need to be examined separately; the action file can only help locate local connections, and cannot replace a comparison of the two sets of input and artifact records.

The Go section does not infer a dependency's purpose from its name, but starts with a small source snippet that directly triggers "Go Direct Dependencies and test-only". PLZ-226 requires saving this input and the tool's actual output. First process this source code through the regular build entry point to confirm whether it truly needs the dependency; then check the same relationship through the test entry point to confirm whether there are additional requirements that arise only during testing. What must be saved here is the result actually produced by the tool, not a classification filled in based on directory location.

| Relationship observed at the time | Materials to retain | Handling during migration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Directly required by the regular entry point | Triggering source code, existing entry point, tool output | Keep it as a direct dependency, then rerun the regular build entry point |
| Required only by the test entry point | Source snippet that triggers the test, tool output | Keep it on the test-only side, run the test entry point separately |
| Visible from both entry points | Output from each entry point | First confirm whether the regular entry point truly needs it, do not promote its classification based solely on how often it appears |

The same dependency appearing at both entry points does not automatically mean it belongs among regular dependencies; passing tests also does not mean the regular build already includes the direct dependency. The migration must prevent two opposite mistakes: promoting a test-only relationship to a regular-build relationship, or mistakenly demoting a relationship already used by the regular entry point to test-only. When the classification changes, first retain its previous location and both types of output, then modify the declaration; this prevents recovery from also undoing the other, correctly configured type of entry point.

PLZ-226 was previously blocked because reproduction had to wait until after Go Rules and Generation's release window. This status only means that the results obtained outside the window at the time were insufficient to confirm integration, not that the dependency relationship had already been determined. Once the window is available, rerun using the saved source code and the original entry point. If the output differs from the old records, first add the differences to the records, then decide whether to adjust the placement of the direct dependency or test-only; do not fold changes to the Go-side classification into the remote-request review results.

Recovery is also split into two tracks. When a remote request produces a reproducible change in results, first restore the call adaptation and old input under the original automation entry point, then check whether the actual artifact matches the baseline record again. If the old entry point can no longer run, still retain the original entry point, commit, and artifact name, and do not substitute a new temporary entry point for the old path. For Go-side recovery, put the dependency back in its pre-migration direct-dependency or test-only location, then trigger the regular build and test entry points separately. If only one entry point is affected, do not roll back the other dependency category.

```text
Old records
  Remote request result changes ──> Investigation around the action
  Go dependency adjustment       ──> All-at-once rollback

Current review
  Remote request input ──> Request metadata ──> Actual artifact
  Triggering source code     ──> Regular build output
               └─> Test entry point output
```

At handoff, attach the job, commit, and artifact name for the remote task, a Go source snippet that triggers the behavior, and the actual output from each of the regular and test entry points. PLZ-209 and PLZ-226 identify these two work items; the validation materials for Native Text File Rules and the release compatibility bridge remain under DOC-23, and are not merged into this record.

Still missing are actual samples of differences in remote request metadata and the Go-section reproduction output after the release window.

# Proposal for Rule Metadata Changes

For this release train, start by separating two issues that are easy to conflate: after Rule metadata Removal, what assessable results old calls can still produce; and where source traversal related to Go installation should stop. Both affect our compatibility guidance, but they should not be bundled into a single conclusion that "the old interface has been cleaned up."

The initial idea is to retain the old calls as counterexamples, without adding new implicit compatibility handling for them. If callers still depend on metadata, we should expose the failure or returned content, then decide whether migration guidance belongs on the rule side or the caller side. At this stage, don't assume "failure" is the only possible outcome: empty returned content, missing fields, and outright errors mean different things to callers.

For the other item, start by checking the source relationships near the installation entry point. Traversal should not continue on to every toolchain or generation rule just because it finds Go files; first identify the objects the install action actually reads, then record one matching and one non-matching boundary example. If the boundary can only be explained using path names, don't change the guidance yet.

src/query/alltargets.go can serve as a nearby starting point for this review. It is in the query package; use it first to confirm which objects are visible on the target-enumeration side, not as proof of where the Go installation implementation belongs.

Still needed: a minimal input for the old metadata call; the object at which installation traversal should stop; whether the two items need separate migration notes.

# Rule Metadata Adjustment Plan

At release-train closeout, Rule metadata Removal and Go source traversal for installation are still handled as two separate tracks. The former focuses on what old calls leave at the public entry point; the latter focuses on which source objects the installation action must reach for a given input. Putting them in one place avoids a release-note misreading of "the rule field has been removed" as "installation-related paths have also been cleaned up."

## Assessment retained from the first draft

The first draft proposed not adding implicit adaptation for old metadata calls; that direction remains. What needs changing is the wording: it is not enough that a caller once read metadata to conclude that the call will fail in a fixed form. The caller may at least encounter a missing field, an empty result, or an exception; migration information should follow the actual result from the entry point. At this stage, do not document any of these forms as established behavior.

The Go installation section should likewise not infer traversal scope from filenames. Go source, toolchain objects, and generated rules found near the installation entry may merely be adjacent objects in the same build graph; include an object in the traversal scope only when it can be shown that the installation action actually reads it. This restriction will make the inspection record shorter, but it avoids treating the directory tree as an interface definition.

## Addendum after a re-review

The PLZ-212 pair has been linked to the support case; reviewing the entry shows the old "Rule metadata Removal" call failing. The trial therefore no longer centers on guessing whether the old field should be retained, but on recording what that path actually returns or throws. Keep the record attached to the entry; do not extrapolate the phenomenon on the card into a claim that all rules fail in the same way.

src/query/alltargets.go remains a navigation point for the re-review. The file header shows that it belongs to `package query`; it can be used to check adjacency relationships related to the target enumeration; it does not replace an actual inspection of the installation path. The earlier claim that query-side objects are evidence for installation traversal is withdrawn.

## Candidate approaches

**Approach A: Change only the rules side.** After metadata is removed, let old calls end with their current results, leaving installation traversal unchanged. The cost is a hard-to-explain gap in the release-train notes: the caller does not know which Go source files the installation entry still reads.

**Approach B: Collect boundary samples first, then decide whether to change the implementation.** Keep one hit and one miss for the installation path. The hit must be an object the entry actually reads; the miss should be an object that appears close but should not be traversed further. At the same time, retain the old call's actual result on the rules side. This approach adds one more review, but does not commit to traversal semantics in advance.

Recommend Approach B. It does not require adding a compatibility layer this round, and it does not treat path names, query enumeration, and installation responsibility as a single basis.

Withdrawal condition: If the old call's observed behavior cannot be reliably attributed to the rule metadata entry point, or if the installation boundary samples can only be inferred from the directory structure, withdraw the proposal to close out the two tracks together and handle them separately. Still to confirm: whether the installation entry ultimately reads a set of source files or already-generated objects; whether multiple variants of the old call are still in use.

# Rule metadata adjustment proposal

Rule metadata Removal and source traversal for Go installation are on the same release train, but the two assessments should remain separate. On the rule side, the question is what compatibility signal legacy calls produce at the entry point; on the installation side, it is what the traversal actually needs to read to complete installation. Directory adjacency cannot answer the former, nor can the presence of a query file determine the latter.

The initial proposal made a convenient but unreliable connection: since `src/query/alltargets.go` can help locate objects related to target enumeration, treat it as the starting point for Go installation traversal. That assessment has been withdrawn. The file belongs to `package query` and is useful as a local navigation aid for the current revision, but that cannot establish where the installation implementation lives, let alone justify describing alltargets' enumeration scope as the install-time source scope.

## Earlier recommendations still on record

The early notes argued that legacy metadata calls should not get any new implicit compatibility handling. That remains the starting point for the trial, but the earlier wording made "no compatibility handling" sound as though uniform failure semantics had already been established. That went too far. Legacy calls may encounter missing fields, empty content, or exceptions; only what the entry point actually returns or throws can determine whether the migration guidance is sufficient. A legacy call failing does not automatically mean that all rules that depend on metadata fail in the same way.

Another earlier recommendation was to "keep traversing when Go source is found." That is no longer being followed either. Toolchains, generation entry points, or rule definitions visible near an installation action are not inherently installation inputs. Without a read relationship, extending traversal along those paths will only misclassify neighbors in the build graph as installation responsibilities.

## Existing review entry points

PLZ-212 records a legacy-call failure during Rule metadata Removal. It is a suitable place to capture the actual result from this invocation of the entry point: record only what was actually returned or thrown, and retain the form of the legacy call that triggered that result. Do not extrapolate beyond the result into a rule compatibility matrix, and do not temporarily restore metadata just because one result is unsatisfactory.

PLZ-229 corresponds to Go Install Source Traversal Boundaries. The check should use the repository's own path entry points and record one hit and one miss: the hit shows that an object is actually read by the installation path; the miss shows that an apparently nearby object was not pulled further into the traversal. The two records serve different purposes; "adjacent paths" cannot substitute for either.

`src/query/alltargets.go` can remain on the review checklist, but only to observe adjacency in target enumeration on the query side. Its connection to the two cards above is navigational adjacency, not a handoff of implementation responsibility. DOC-26 records alltargets Implicit Target Cleanup and input-traversal fallback, and should be kept as separate operational response material; its troubleshooting branches are not reproduced here.

## This trial

The recommendation is to proceed in the following order, rather than change the implementation first and explain it afterward:

1. Start from the legacy call in PLZ-212 and capture one complete result from the entry point. If content is returned, record the parts directly related to the missing metadata; if an exception is thrown, record where it occurred. If there is no result, do not fill the gap with an expected error.
2. Start from the installation path in PLZ-229 and select one source-read record that is a confirmed hit. Then select a miss record for an adjacent object. Both records must come from checks using the same criteria; otherwise, they cannot establish at which step the traversal stopped.
3. Review the two records side by side. The rule record answers how the legacy call ended; the installation record answers why input traversal continued or stopped. Only discuss whether the caller or installation implementation needs to be changed once both are clear.

The trade-off is clear. Simply deleting metadata and declaring compatibility work complete requires the fewest changes, but leaves the specific outcomes of legacy calls and the installation traversal boundary for later investigation. Conversely, adding compatibility fields for legacy calls or including all adjacent Go source in installation traversal might look like a way to reduce short-term failures, but would expand the interface and installation inputs, with no evidence that this expansion is necessary.

The preference at this stage is therefore not to add an implicit compatibility layer or expand traversal scope; first capture a reviewable sample from each of the two entry points. This preference is not a general conclusion about all Go rules; it applies only to the legacy metadata calls and installation paths observed in this trial.

## When to stop the trial

If any of the following occurs, stop treating the two pieces of work as a single closeout item:

- The legacy call in PLZ-212 does not consistently reproduce the same entry-point behavior, or it is not possible to determine whether the actual result was caused by metadata removal;
- An installation-path hit can only be inferred from file location, and the read operation cannot be established;
- An object considered a miss is later shown to be read by another installation branch;
- The only way to make the legacy call pass is to restore the removed metadata, rather than adjust the caller.

If the first case occurs, the rule-side issue should be kept separate, and "legacy call failure" should not be stated as a release conclusion. If any of the other cases occurs, a separate implementation investigation should be opened into the installation traversal boundary; query adjacency records no longer serve as supporting evidence.

Two questions remain unresolved: whether the final object read by the installation entry point is a set of source files or a generated object; and whether there are variants of legacy metadata calls that do not go through this entry point. The former determines how the boundary sample is described; the latter determines whether migration guidance can be placed at just one entry point. Until both points are confirmed, do not submit changes that expand traversal or restore fields.

# alltargets Fallback Troubleshooting Tree

This record has long been used in regression investigations for the compatibility train, not because it provides a fixed set of answers, but because it is the starting point for examining two phenomena that can easily obscure each other: the alltargets output contains something that should not be listed as an ordinary target, or input traversal has already entered a fallback state, yet the result is still interpreted as an ordinary enumeration. The former looks like cleanup missed an entry; the latter looks more like the query process lost its original input conditions. The old record combined them into a single handling path, but the later review did not retain that grouping.

The starting point for review is still `src/query/alltargets.go`. The file belongs to the `query` package, and an import block is visible at the top of the file; these facts only indicate that the investigation should start on the query side, not that every state of input traversal can be attributed to this file. When someone investigating an incident has only a single line of anomalous output, first fill in the target expression for that request, the complete target set returned, whether fallback occurred, and which inputs were retained before and after fallback. Do not delete apparently redundant targets first and then try to guess whether they were internal items.

```text
Received an alltargets anomaly
|
+-- Are there apparently implicit entries in the output?
|   |
|   +-- Yes: save the original target set
|   |   |      |
|   |   |      +-- Does the entry appear only at the end of the result?
|   |   |      |   Do not conclude from this that it is a sorting issue; look back at the set before filtering.
|   |   |      |
|   |   |      +-- Does the entry appear across multiple results?
|   |   |          Check whether it comes from ordinary target enumeration or an internal construction path.
|   |
|   +-- No: turn to input traversal.
|
+-- Is there evidence of fallback in input traversal?
    |
    +-- No: check the locations of filtering and result assembly within the alltargets path.
    |
    +-- Yes: save the pre-fallback input, post-fallback input, and final result separately;
        do not treat the final result directly as an enumeration of the original input.
```

Assessment from the initial draft (retained): the fallback state is determined solely by alltargets, so locating the result cleanup point in `src/query/alltargets.go` is enough to classify the anomalous output as incomplete cleanup of implicit targets. This was written that way at the time to give the on-call staff an initial place to start; it was reasonably usable for cases where "extra internal items appear in the output", but it did not cover cases where input traversal had already changed the query conditions. This passage has not been deleted because someone later followed precisely this old assessment, checked only the end of the result, and missed the inconsistency between the inputs before and after fallback.

The later review added a narrower distinction: first determine whether the anomaly is "extra content in the target set itself" or "the input used to form the set has already fallen back". Both can happen at the same time, but evidence from the incident for one cannot substitute for evidence for the other. An extra entry in one result does not imply that input traversal did not fall back; likewise, observing a fallback state does not imply that every extra entry in the result was caused by fallback. Separate these two questions first so that subsequent investigation does not repeatedly apply different interpretations to the same output.

## What to Preserve First

When the output is suspected of containing implicit targets, save the full output rather than extracting the suspicious lines. In particular, preserve the target scope originally specified in the request and the relative positions of ordinary targets and suspicious entries in the result. Relative position is not evidence of causation, but it can prevent the next investigator from combining two results into one. If all that remains from the incident is a secondhand report that "there was an extra target", do not label it "cleanup failure" before obtaining the original output again.

When input traversal falls back, separate at least three parts: the input when traversal began, the input still visible when fallback was confirmed, and the input ultimately passed to query result processing. This separation is intended to let investigators distinguish whether the state change occurred before or after result generation. Without these three parts, continuing to experiment with filtering on alltargets results is meaningless; it can only produce cleaner output, not establish what the original target set should have been.

The old record treated "rerun the same query once" as a recovery action. This action can only confirm whether the anomaly recurs; it cannot restore the input replaced by fallback or prove which stage the internal items came from. Rerunning is still allowed after the review, but retain the respective input descriptions and complete results before and after the rerun; if the inputs to the two requests are already different, do not draw conclusions about the filtering logic from the differences in their results.

## Branch Starting from the Output

When a suspicious item appears in the output, first ask whether it is an ordinary target that should be listed for this request. Here, "ordinary targets" means only the targets the caller expects to receive from alltargets, excluding objects that exist briefly during internal construction. If the evidence from the incident does not allow this distinction, record it as "object source unconfirmed", not "implicit target leak".

If the suspicious item appears consistently in the results, inspect the point in the alltargets path where the result set is formed, then check whether cleanup or filtering runs afterward. Only the relative order of adjacent steps needs to be confirmed; when there is insufficient material, do not assign specific functions responsibilities they do not have. The `query` package containing the file is the current entry point, which does not mean that it implements the entire input traversal.

If the suspicious item appears only after fallback, do not fix the result directly yet. Record it as "the post-fallback set contains this item" and return to the input side. The easiest mistake at this point is to interpret the final set as an ordinary enumeration and then tighten the cleanup conditions. That may reduce the visible output while also excluding targets that should still have been retained. The older handling guidance did not make this stopping point explicit, and it was added here after the review was carried out.

If the result contains no internal items but its count, coverage, or duplication is unexpected, first check whether the input fell back as well. The alltargets result is not a list generated independently of its input; when fallback occurs, even a result with no obvious "dirty entries" may no longer correspond to the target scope originally received. This branch only requires deciding whether to continue investigating the input side, not establishing the cause of the traversal state on this page.

## Branch Starting from Input Fallback

After confirming evidence of fallback, first stop temporary "deduplication" or "implicit item removal" on the final output. The input sets before and after fallback must each be retained, even if one part is empty or incompletely recorded. A blank is meaningful in itself: it means the investigation did not capture that layer, not that the layer did not change.

Next, check only one thing: whether final result processing received the pre-fallback input, the post-fallback input, or an indistinguishable mixed state. If fallback can be confirmed but the handoff point cannot, leave the anomaly at "relationship between input state and result unconfirmed". Do not infer where the handoff occurred from the filename, and do not substitute the behavior of another query for the input record of this alltargets request.

A seemingly complete result after fallback is not evidence that fallback had no effect. Conversely, if the output suddenly narrows, it cannot be classified directly as excessive cleanup without the original input. For either phenomenon, first return to the three retained parts of the input. Until enough of the incident context has been recovered to compare these three parts, any result-side fix is only a provisional guess.

## Shortcut Assessments That No Longer Apply

"As long as the result contains no obvious internal items, there is no need to investigate input traversal." This was a shortcut assessment in the initial draft that no longer applies. It suited the situation at the time, when only explicitly anomalous entries were being handled, but it misses scope changes caused by fallback.

"It has to be either implicit-target cleanup or input fallback." This is another old simplification. The review did not prove that the two are related in every incident, so they cannot instead be bound together as the sole cause. The current approach is simply to retain the evidence separately, then decide whether to continue on the result side or the input side first.

"Finding the adjacent code in `src/query/alltargets.go` is enough to close the issue." This sentence is retained as a pointer to the old entry point, but it must not be treated as a condition for stopping work. The file is a starting point for verification; when the inputs before and after fallback have not been recorded, reading only the local result-side code is not enough to reconstruct the incident.

## When to Stop

Stop making further changes to the results in the following cases:

- The original output has been lost, leaving only a secondhand report;
- Input fallback is known to have occurred, but the inputs before and after fallback cannot be distinguished;
- The source of the suspicious entry is still unconfirmed and can only be guessed from its display position;
- After inspecting the local alltargets path, it is still unclear whether the result set was formed before or after fallback.

Stopping does not mean the anomaly has disappeared. Retain the target scope of this request, whether the full output exists, whether a fallback state has been observed, and the entry point already inspected, `src/query/alltargets.go`. If the original input or complete result can be obtained later, continue from the corresponding branch. What is retained here is the troubleshooting practice from the compatibility train; this record has not codified all input traversal scenarios into current rules.

# Go Toolchain Version Decision Record

This page's earliest recorded conclusion was straightforward: Go Toolchain Platforms and Minimum Versions belongs to the installation toolchain; start by looking at `tools/please_go_install/toolchain/toolchain.go`. The early wording did not label this conclusion as a working assumption, so it reads as though the requirement already had a clear owner. That wording later made it easy to mistake the file path for the responsibility boundary, so while retaining the old paragraphs, this review also records the limitations it found.

The file header actually provides only `package toolchain` and a set of imports. This indicates that this is a local entry point in the toolchain package; it cannot, based on this alone, establish that platform determination, the minimum version, the installation action, and the caller are all handled in the same file. The earlier investigation reached this point from the issue name and call name; the value of this path is to narrow the scope, not to replace the actual references.

## Where the Old Interpretation Came From

At the time, the team was organizing installation issues in the cumulative compatibility train. The platform and minimum version were placed under the same requirement history, so it was natural to treat the toolchain file nearest the installation name as the landing point. One practical benefit of this choice was that searchers did not have to guess the entry point in the broad build graph first; they could first confirm which declarations and adjacent objects existed in the package.

But "near installation" is not proof of ownership. The filename may only reflect the package's organization, and `import` only indicates a local dependency. The early record compressed these two observations into "toolchain.go is responsible," omitting the intermediate reference check. That omission is exactly why the page later appeared overly certain.

The early version also treated "platform" and "minimum version" as one inseparable installation item. This made them easy to track in the requirements list, but did not answer whether the two determinations came from the same configuration location or whether a change to one would require the other to change in sync. No implementation material sufficient to separate them was left here, so the old record should not be treated as a field or interface definition.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

The record actually contained three possible approaches. The first was to keep the determination local to the toolchain: it was closest to the file originally found and made the fewest changes to the original investigation entry point. The cost was that, if an installation or configuration path existed that did not go through this package, an investigator might see only an indirect result.

The second was to move the platform and minimum version up into a unified configuration. This would make the configuration closure more centralized and make it relatively easier to find similar constraints when tracing a requirement back. However, there was no material at the time to confirm whether installation behavior and ordinary build configuration were suitable for sharing the same landing point; moving them up directly might only move the uncertainty to a broader location.

The third was to retain the item only in the requirement record without pointing to a code file for now. It would not create an incorrect implementation ownership assignment, but it could not provide a starting point for people who later searched the code. For a compatibility train, this would leave the issue at the description layer, and a later review would still have to search again from the name.

At the time, the choice was a weaker version of the first: use `tools/please_go_install/toolchain/toolchain.go` as the verification starting point, without moving the requirement or recording an unsupported minimum-version value. The original text stated this decision more strongly than the facts warranted, as if the file already carried the complete determination; what was actually recorded was only the investigation order.

This order was to inspect local declarations and direct references first, then check the configuration closure involved in the change, and only then decide which file should carry the requirement. Without reference snippets, do not split the platform and minimum version into two implementation points that had already been completed, and do not rewrite the requirement name as a code fact. It is a decision to defer ownership, not a completed configuration decision.

## Correction After Review

A later addendum to PLZ-216 pointed out that the Installation And Toolchain section still had one unconfirmed point. This correction did not provide a specific minimum version or a complete configuration closure; it only rejected the most likely misreading caused by the old page: "finding the file already means that responsibility has been confirmed."

Therefore, the old statement of local ownership should be read as historical wording: it explains why the investigation began with the toolchain package, but cannot serve as the basis for the change location. The file may still participate in platform or version determination, or it may simply be a local package along the path. The available material is insufficient to reach a new affirmative conclusion between those possibilities.

This review did not overturn the early decision as a whole. Keeping the entry point is still useful because it keeps the search focused near the installation toolchain; what was withdrawn was the step of jumping directly from the entry point to the "sole implementation." For anyone who needs to revisit the judgment made at the time, this distinction is more important than adding an unverified final conclusion.

## Verification Status

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> LocalEntry
    LocalEntry: tools/please_go_install/toolchain/toolchain.go
    LocalEntry --> ReferenceReview
    ReferenceReview: Verify actual references
    ReferenceReview --> ConfigClosure
    ConfigClosure: Check configuration closure
    ConfigClosure --> OwnershipDecision
    OwnershipDecision: Determine requirement ownership
    OwnershipDecision --> [*]
```

The order in the diagram is not an implementation flowchart; it is the verification sequence left by this old decision. First confirm that the local declarations in the file still correspond to the record, then follow the actual references to determine whether it enters the path related to Installation And Toolchain. If the references cannot carry the requirement object to that location, do not continue to treat it as proof of ownership merely because the filename is similar.

The configuration closure is the second checkpoint. The description of PLZ-216 requires checking the configuration closure involved in the change, with any missing item traced to the corresponding repository file. This means the card provides a direction for tracing back, not evidence that the toolchain package already contains all configuration. Interpreting the card's wording directly as file responsibility would repeat the same error in the early record.

Only then should ownership be addressed. If both the actual references and the configuration closure lead back to the local toolchain area, it is only then permissible to record what object is carried here; if either one lands elsewhere, the requirement history should point to that actual file, rather than being forced to remain at the current path just to preserve consistency with the old page. No such reference or configuration snippets were saved here, so no fabricated conclusion is written.

## Old Assessment of Compatibility Cost

Early on, there was concern that although keeping the determination inside the toolchain package would keep the change surface smaller, other entry points might only observe an indirect result; although moving the determination upward would make centralized inspection easier, it might mix installation-only behavior with broader configuration. These two were risks considered when comparing the options, not regression records of things that had already happened.

The meaning of "minimum version" was also not disentangled on this page. It might be the threshold for installing the toolchain, or a platform constraint in the compatibility train. If the two were written directly as one definite configuration, later people would mistakenly believe that modifying the installer had completed all compatibility work; if they were completely disconnected, the original association would be lost when tracing the requirement back. The old record chose not to fill in a value, retaining only the object name and local entry point.

This choice did not resolve the requirement; it only avoided filling the gap with guesses. It also left the page for a long time in an uncomfortable but accurate state: the early interpretation appeared decisive, while the review only withdrew the overly strong ownership inference and did not replace it with a new complete decision.

## Decision Retained

The decision currently retained is narrow: tracing Go Toolchain Platforms and Minimum Versions back begins at `tools/please_go_install/toolchain/toolchain.go`; the path itself does not constitute proof of a platform determination, minimum version, or complete configuration closure. When continuing this item, first retrieve the actual references and configuration materials in the order shown in the diagram, then decide where the requirement lands.

This record is no longer suitable as the basis for "toolchain.go is the sole ownership location," but the old judgment is not being removed. It records why this entry point was chosen at the beginning of the compatibility train and also preserves the unconfirmed point found later. The specific minimum version, complete reference relationships, and final file ownership are still not finalized here.

# nocache Parameter Retirement Proposal

The subject of this review is 2026.09 Cumulative Compatibility Train's `nocache` parameter. The original idea was to remove it from external calls to avoid carrying forward a branch after the upgrade that no longer had a clear explanation; at the time, though, there weren't enough records to show that all callers had migrated away from it. This page is therefore being kept as a trial proposal, not a notice that retirement is complete.

Check `src/query/whatoutputs_test.go` first. The earlier investigation started at a query-side test seam, which can help locate the parameter-related inputs and result comparison points. Don't infer implementation ownership from filenames alone, and don't treat test files as a caller inventory. What's missing: the entry points that actually read `nocache` at that revision, the callers still passing it, and whether the upgrade really introduced a regression in the results.

The preferred trial approach has two steps. First, don't immediately remove the parsing or compatibility branch. Only change the calls in the new version so they no longer explicitly pass `nocache`, while keeping a path for observing old calls. Second, compare results before and after the upgrade using the same set of inputs, and record the commands, versions, and failure points. If the results match, then discuss removing the compatibility handling; if the results change, keep the old path and don't attribute the differences to the parameter's retirement itself.

The review compared two options: removing the parameter outright means a small change and a clean interface, but any remaining old calls would only surface at runtime; retaining the parameter for a while carries more compatibility overhead, but allows unmigrated calls to be identified. No decision was made here on the length of the compatibility window or which caller should switch first. Whether `nocache` affects only query results, and whether it also affects other outputs after the upgrade, still need to be confirmed from actual references.

The rollback conditions are narrow: if calls without the parameter produce unexplained differences in results, or a caller is found that still needs the old parameter, stop the removal, restore the original calling pattern, and retain the failing inputs and version information. Don't close this issue based on a single successful run; at a minimum, keep the failure points and rerun commands.

Open items

- [ ] Complete the list of actual references to `nocache` and its callers.
- [ ] Record a before-and-after upgrade comparison to confirm whether the "regression in results" is reproducible.
- [ ] Decide how long to retain the compatibility branch and who approves its final removal.

If the only follow-up completed is checking the test files, this page still only identifies an entry point for the trial; it does not establish that the parameter has been retired.

# Dependency Boundary Audit: Consumer FAQ

**Where should consumers look first?**

Start at `docs/adj-parse/faq/parse-dependency-boundary-audit-three-questions-left-by-users.md` as before. That page is adj-parse's latest-known export; the project continues to maintain the body and attachments. When taking over, first provide the entry point and revision you saw, then add the first symptom you observed. A screenshot or an old link alone isn't enough to tell whether two entry points with the same name come from the same source.

**Why not merge sources by name?**

The audit covers dependency sources around license, not display names. Adoption scope and responsibility for retirement are also recorded separately. PLZA-001 require separate records of the source and adopters for each of the two current entry points; in PLZA-008, the search for the earliest source that can be reconstructed is still working back through `parse-supply-boundary`'s revisions. Without that part of the chain, don't record speculation as a conclusion about the source.

**What must be recorded separately during handoff?**

"Current entry point" refers only to the page or link the consumer actually opened; "current revision" is used to trace the source back through `parse-supply-boundary`. Neither can be inferred from the name. An old link can help locate the relevant context, but it can't replace the source chain; likewise, a screenshot without an adopter and a version can't prove that the two entry points have been merged. When the entry point crosses over to a shared interface, just record the handoff point; subsequent compatibility assessments are still up to that interface's maintainer.

**Who is responsible for answering "Is anyone still using it?"**

First look for teams still using adj-parse. PLZA-007 record that search; even if no consumers are found in the end, record the search scope. The project's own maintainer handles adoption scope and exit criteria. When crossing over to a shared interface, hand over only the reproduction entry point; don't transfer scheduling for the whole effort.

**What if the source can't be found?**

The approach in PLZA-015 is to look for evidence that can be used to reconstruct adj-parse; without evidence, hide the explanation rather than fill in a seemingly complete assessment. PLZA-001, PLZA-007, PLZA-008, and PLZA-015 retain clues about entry-point separation, the last consumer, source tracing, and missing sources, respectively. They must not be consolidated into a list of adopters. DOC-33 contain records from still-open cases that can be used to check for any new leads specific to those cases.

**Are there any unanswered questions?**

Yes. The build graph still hasn't been added; the available material doesn't establish that an unlisted consumer has stopped using it.

# parse-supply-boundary Troubleshooting Tree

Trigger: the entry point already shows a problem, but it's not yet clear whether this is a dependency-source, exit-action, or permissions issue. Preserve the first failing sample and the environment differences at the time before proceeding; don't clear the state just to get new output, and don't retry first and then go back looking for the original symptoms.

The entry-point file is at `docs/adj-parse/runbooks/parse-supply-boundary-who-to-handoff-to-when-blocked.md`. First confirm that what you're seeing concerns the dependency boundary, rather than notes left over from a neighboring page. If the page has no text identifying the object being handled, stop here; fill in the entry-point information before continuing. Don't infer ownership from the name.

## First Decision

If `parse-supply-boundary` is already visible at the entry point, check whether both the dependency source and the scope of use are recorded alongside it.

- Both are present: keep the symptom on the dependency-boundary branch and continue checking whether the source description matches the entry point.
- Only the source is visible, with no scope of use: don't turn this into an exit-action issue. Record that the scope of use is missing, and stop here.
- Only the scope of use is visible, and the source is unclear: don't fill in a possible license or dependency name. Preserve the existing excerpt and wait for source material.
- Neither is present: go back to the entry page and look for them; if they're still missing, stop. Don't forward this to the final handler.

`rule parameters` is only a signal to keep examining the boundary description, not the cause itself. Leave it unchanged when you see it; without evidence linking it to the object being handled, don't expand the investigation based on the parameter name.

## Exit-Action Branch

If the dependency source can be identified but the page doesn't specify an exit action, move to the exit-action branch. Record the specific gap: is the rollback command missing, or is the stop condition missing? Neither can substitute for the other.

If a rollback command is documented but no stop condition is given, pause at the missing stop condition. If it only says "rollback required" without an executable action, treat that as a missing exit action too. Don't assume the recovery steps have already been tried in the shared environment. If the record has no verification results, don't run recovery against the environment; only keep a record of where verification is pending.

## Permissions Branch

If the entry point explicitly points to a restricted detail page but you can't view the required content, hand it to the permissions owner with the first failing sample and the entry point you accessed. An old link in a regular directory is not the same case as a restricted detail page: for an old link, first return to the corresponding record and find a usable entry point; for a restricted page, don't refresh repeatedly, and don't record an access failure as a dependency-resolution failure.

If the page opens but `target tag` doesn't appear, stop at the missing tag. At this point, it's still unclear whether old and new records are mixed, the tag wasn't generated, or the entry point targets the wrong object. Don't skip this step and decide on the dependency source or exit path.

## What to Leave in the Handoff

Include only the branch you're on, the first failing sample, the environment differences, and where you stopped. # Compatibility Directory Route Proposal

This proposal retains a candidate path that was not added to the directory currently in use. It was not originally intended to rename core; rather, within the same compatibility record, the generation entry point and the failure exit did not appear to be the same kind of thing. The old draft framed the choice as continuing with `Go rules` or splitting `remote action` out separately; the preference at the time was to split it. That preference is retained here. It must not be recast as already adopted, and there is not enough evidence to judge the other path wrong.

## The Two Paths Still on the Table

Continuing with `Go rules` has the benefit of fewer entry points, so existing usage does not have to be moved first. The cost is that different failure exits remain crowded into the same record; when a fork appears, it remains difficult to say whether the cause is the rule itself, the generation entry point, or the caller's `toolchain`. Splitting `remote action` out separately has the benefit that their respective inputs and failure exits can be recorded separately; the cost is maintaining a compatibility bridge, with the labels, request metadata, and version chain between the old and new entry points all needing to be cross-checked. It has not been confirmed that all existing callers can use the compatibility bridge, nor who would maintain the generation entry point after the split.

Therefore, the old draft chose the latter, but that choice went no further than a trial proposal; it was not a directory rule. The trial is limited to the core-compatibility-catalog path and must not also change the entry points of neighboring projects. For a comparison, keep the current entry point, user, input, and observation window fixed, and replace only the current revision. PLZB-005 later turned this restriction into a card action: keep core-compatibility-catalog, the current entry point, and the command fixed, and replace only the current revision. Scope was confirmed on January 6, and work did not start until January 7; the interval between those two actions must not be treated as already having a result.

## What to Leave Behind During the Trial

For each side, first save the raw input, the revision used, the first visible result, and the generation command and the time it was run. Changing only the display label does not count as a valid comparison; if only one side has run and there is no feedback from a real user, that cannot support a claim that the issue was pinpointed faster. The observation windows on both sides must be the same; otherwise, "easier to find" may simply mean that one side was opened first.

This originally said, "same user, same input, change only one condition." Retain the sentence as a proposal constraint, but there is no corresponding caller list. The gap left unresolved in the live environment at the time was `request metadata`: it was unclear whether it should be passed along with the old entry point or regenerated by the split-out path. The `generation entry point` has also not been confirmed from the reverse direction; the proposal must not assume that it is the compatibility bridge's only landing point.

The criterion is not a single green result. If both the time to pinpoint the issue and the misclassification count show no improvement, the trial should end; if a difference can be produced only by changing labels, the result is invalid; and if `target label` cannot be restored on exit, the scope must not be expanded. Stop at the current interface boundary; do not turn unconfirmed callers into a support list.

## The Actual Gap in the Record

On January 20, PLZB-012 left "qa_reproduced"; its card required comparing the generation commands and the times they were run for two core · Compatibility Catalog entries and stopping at the first fork. This result can only show that the comparison window did in fact reproduce the fork; it does not show which route won. On January 21, it was marked blocked, with the reason, "This window is closed; run it again during the next maintenance cycle." So v2 added reruns and window records, but did not rewrite the blocked status as a proposal conclusion.

The timing of the resource loan also cannot be filled in from memory. The registration entry for PLZB-010 requires the borrower, start time, and return window for the current revision to be written back to the original card; the proposal treats this only as a trial cost and does not claim that registration is complete. If this is missing, it is difficult at exit to determine whether the route failed or the resource was not returned within the window.

The old draft also listed the "build graph" as a visible comparison item on the other side, and left `bootstrap`, `sandbox helper`, and the version chain as terms to investigate. These do not form a complete implementation description on this page: the build graph is only a candidate observation surface, while bootstrap and sandbox helper are merely unresolved terms from the live environment. If the meanings of these terms later need to change, leave a separate record with results; do not use this proposal to fill in the gaps.

## Rollback Points and Open Items

On rollback, restore the original entry point first, then retain the raw input, revision, command, and first fork already collected; do not just delete the displayed result. Stop expanding the trial if any of the following occurs: the time to pinpoint the issue has not improved, misclassification has not decreased, the old entry point cannot be restored on exit, or a caller requires an interface that has not been confirmed. Restoring the old entry point does not confirm that the old route is better; it only means that this candidate did not meet the condition for continuing to occupy the window.

Still undecided are: the list of existing `toolchain` callers, ownership of `request metadata`, the maintenance boundary of the compatibility bridge, the result of the reverse check on the `generation entry point`, and the borrow-and-return record for the current revision. The long-term owner is also not settled in this proposal. DOC-36 can serve as adjacent troubleshooting material, but it does not answer these questions here; this page retains the old proposal, which favored splitting and later stopped when the rerun window closed.

# Quality Signal Console Dual-State Postmortem

Quality Signal Console displayed two states for the same object during a check of a failed sample formed around test. The initial record only noted that the current revision seen on either side of the entry point differed, and did not retain a continuous trail sufficient to attribute the discrepancy to a specific stage. The output directory was later restored, and the incident was briefly treated as closed; this version records post-recovery availability separately from whether the state discrepancy disappeared.

## What Still Holds from the Earlier Incident

The original record remains. It shows that the state of the same object cannot be judged solely by the result of the latest inspection, and that failed samples cannot be removed from regression stratification just because they recovered later. When two states appear, unstable-signal attribution loses a reliable input as a result: if the same sample receives different descriptions from different entry points, that alone cannot be used to judge it stable or unstable.

It was not confirmed at the time whether the compatibility bridge was involved. That assessment has not been changed to "the compatibility bridge caused the problem"; it remains only a direction for investigation. The only recovery fact that can be confirmed now is that the output directory was restored to service. The recovery page cannot replace the original record, and the original record cannot be backfilled to say that the root cause has been found.

## Timeline Added This Time

| Relative position | Record left behind | What could be concluded then |
|---|---|---|
| Initial divergence | The same object showed two states | Record the two entry points and the current revision seen at each |
| After the original record was saved | The failed sample remained in regression stratification | Do not overwrite the original sample with a retry result |
| Output directory restored | User path available again | Record recovery only; do not close attribution |
| Subsequent check | Current result has no source attached | This result cannot be merged into the original diagnosis |

The PLZC-011 action first confirmed that after recovery, the first current revision should be captured rather than using a later aggregation to replace the incident evidence. The action addressed the record boundary: the first record after the recovery point can serve as the starting point for the recovery page, but cannot be used retroactively to explain what happened at the first divergence.

The PLZC-010 action later classified the anomaly as a failed-sample issue and left a reminder: "the current result has no source attached." Here, "source" means which entry point and which record this current result came from; without that association, the standalone state text cannot be compared with the earlier saved version. The earlier retelling that contained only a screenshot did not fill this gap, so it was not used as an attribution basis.

The PLZC-012 handoff record stopped at the first broken link. This stopping point is important to preserve: it shows that the handoff can proceed from the execution record to the current result, but cannot continue to establish when the two first became inconsistent. Describing the portion after the broken link as a state synchronization delay would turn an unconfirmed process into a fact.

```text
Original failed sample
      |
      v
Regression stratification -----> State record A
      |                               |
      |                               +---- Current revisions differ
      v
Unstable-signal attribution -> State record B

Recovery page: output directory available
Attribution page: still unconfirmed
```

## Restating the Impact

This is not the conclusion that "all regression stratification is wrong." Available evidence covers only the failed samples formed around this test and the state discrepancies those samples encountered when entering regression stratification and unstable-signal attribution. The separate schedule, maintenance owner, and exit criteria remain with Quality Signal Console, but they do not replace an explanation of the dual state.

Three impacts are clear.

- The original failed samples must continue to be retained. They are the only incident evidence available when the discrepancy was observed that had not gone through later aggregation.
- Regression stratification must not collapse the two states into a single "final state." This would lose the entry-point difference and make later readers assume that all records came from the same current revision.
- Unstable-signal attribution needs to include the source of the state. A current result without a source can only be treated as information pending verification; it cannot independently serve as an attribution basis.

The unresolved points also remain here: it is not known how long each of the two states lasted, whether any other objects were affected in the same way, or why the compatibility bridge changed. The recovery action did not answer these questions.

## Handling and Stop Point

The handling of the incident did not involve continuing to retry until only one state remained. After the discrepancy was first seen, the original input and entry-point version were saved; after the output directory was restored, a separate recovery record was opened; when the current result could not be linked back to the original record, processing stopped. This was more useful than blending multiple rounds of results into a single smooth timeline, because the latter would conceal the boundary of this anomaly.

The PLZC-010, PLZC-011 and PLZC-012 entries serve only as entry points for related addenda. They respectively cover the unrecorded window, the first current revision after recovery, and the confirmation time in the on-call handoff. The card actions show that the addendum was initiated, but do not add a causal conclusion absent from the original incident evidence.

What still needs to be filled is not a generalized process, but these specific gaps:

1. The time gap between the first appearance of state A and state B.
2. The current revision used by each of the two entry points.
3. Whether the output directory becoming available again and the state records becoming consistent again occurred at the same time.
4. Whether the compatibility bridge had a corresponding change during this window.
5. Whether the first broken link where the handoff stopped can be reconnected using the original record or the recovery page.
