The action taken at the time was to preserve the original record, and to stop using further retries to eliminate the discrepancy. The reason for this action was not that retries were necessarily useless, but that each additional retry might leave only a new current result, while obscuring the original relationship between the entry point, the current revision, and the failure sample. If only a single post-recovery record were ultimately saved, later readers would only know "available now," but would not see why the status could not previously be attributed directly to the object itself.

The original record did not contain complete timestamps. That gap still exists. The "first divergence" cannot be assigned to a specific moment, nor can the duration of the dual-state condition be inferred from the recovery page. This postmortem preserves the relative sequence without inventing precise times: the divergence was observed first, then the incident evidence was saved, then the output directory was restored, and only afterward did a current result with a gap in its provenance appear.

```text
Failure samples
   |
   +--> Regression stratification -----> Entry point 1: Status A
   |                         |
   |                         +--> Current revision differs from the other entry point
   |
   +--> Unstable-signal attribution -> Entry point 2: Status B

Recovery page: Output directory available
Cause page: Compatibility bridge change unconfirmed
```

The two entry-point lines in the diagram do not describe new execution paths, but simply bring together the two observational perspectives that must both be preserved in this record. The names Status A and Status B do not appear in the original material; these two placeholder labels are used to avoid mistakenly placing a later current result back into the incident snapshot from the first divergence.

## Where the Impact Was Felt

There is not enough material from this incident to establish an impact scope covering all objects. The available material supports conclusions only about the failure samples created around test in this incident, the regression stratification containing those samples, and the status inconsistency exposed when they entered unstable-signal attribution. There is no basis for extending the conclusion to other projects, nor can the restoration of the output directory be used to retroactively claim that all historical samples have been corrected.

For failing samples, the impact is that retention semantics have changed. They can no longer be retained based solely on a single state seen later; at a minimum, they must be retained along with the entry point where they were first seen and the current revision. Otherwise, the same failing sample will appear inconsistent in subsequent curation, when in fact records from different points in time have simply been merged.

For regression stratification, the impact is that the stratification criteria must accommodate cases of "the same object, different entry points, different current revisions". This does not call for establishing a new classification scheme, but for avoiding prematurely collapsing two states into a single final state. Collapsing them would make the stratification look clean, but would erase the most valuable information from this anomaly: the state differences are not stable differences verified within the same original record, but differences observed across entry points and times.

For attribution of unstable signals, the impact is more direct. Attribution requires knowing where a state came from; a state without an entry point and current revision can only show that someone saw a result at some point, not explain why a failing sample was considered unstable. It is acceptable to retain this current result as an annotation, but not to treat it as a standalone attribution conclusion.

For the recovery page, the impact is that recovery records must remain restrained. Recovery of the output directory indicates that the path is usable again. It does not indicate that the dual-state condition has disappeared, does not indicate that historical records will automatically align, and does not indicate that the compatibility bridge has not changed. Recovery is recorded separately precisely to prevent "usable" from replacing "explained".

## Why the two versions of the records cannot overwrite each other

The early version of this page kept the original record, the recovery page, and unconfirmed causes separate, a choice made when the available material was insufficient. At that time, the easiest mistake to make was to overwrite the failure scene with green output from the next run. Subsequent additions to the record show that this choice remains correct: the current post-recovery result has no source attached and cannot be linked back to the record from the initial deviation.

The "source" here is not a generic indication of origin, but the entry point and record location corresponding to the current result. Without this relationship, a state cannot be compared against the original failing sample, nor can it be determined whether it belongs to before recovery, after recovery, or a subsequent summary. Earlier accounts containing only screenshots did not resolve this issue. A screenshot can show that a particular state was once observed, but cannot show that it and the state from another entry point were observed under the same conditions.

The supplemental records from PLZC-011 provide a limited but useful rule: starting at the point of recovery, use only the first current revision entry and leave subsequent summaries aside for now. This is not intended to elevate the first record to root-cause evidence, but to prevent post-recovery summaries from being written back to the point of recovery. The first record at least preserves "what the entry point saw when recovery first appeared"; later curation results may already include new state changes.

After PLZC-010, it was classified as a failing-sample issue. This classification helped narrow the discussion from general entry-point anomalies to the objects that the quality signal dashboard actually handles: failing samples related to test and their stratification and attribution. It did not confirm that the compatibility bridge was the cause, nor did it confirm that every stratification state was affected. The card retains the note "the current result has no source attached", so this version treats the missing source as an open item rather than using the act of classification as a substitute for a conclusion about the cause.

PLZC-012 records the handoff moving from execution records to the first break in the chain, then stopping at the current result. This stopping point shows that the handoff chain was not completely lost: an existing execution record can be used to locate a current state; however, there is no material either before or after that point that can connect it to the original incident context. Writing down the stopping point is more accurate than continuing to guess whether the chain broke at the compatibility bridge, the entry point, or the object state itself.

Each of the three supplemental-recording entry points has its own boundary: PLZC-011 is the first record after recovery, PLZC-010 is the no-record window and source gap, and PLZC-012 is the handoff confirmation and chain-break location. They can help review the same event, but they cannot be combined into a causal chain that has already been closed.

## Timeline

| Order | Known record | Conclusion strength | What should not be inferred from this |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The same object displayed two states at two entry points | Direct observation | Cannot conclude that the object itself simultaneously had two stable states |
| 2 | Two entry-point views showed different current revisions | Direct observation | Cannot conclude that the difference was necessarily caused by the revision |
| 3 | The original record was retained and not further overwritten by retries | Action already executed | Cannot conclude that subsequent retries had no value |
| 4 | The output directory was restored for use | Recovery result already achieved | Cannot conclude that the root cause has disappeared |
| 5 | The first current revision after recovery was extracted separately | Supplemental-recording rule | Cannot let a later summary replace it |
| 6 | The current result exists, but no source is attached | Later discovery | Cannot treat this result as part of the original diagnosis |
| 7 | The handoff stopped at the first break in the chain | Recorded stopping point | Cannot fill in the causes after the break in the chain |

The timeline does not use absolute timestamps because the time gap for the first deviation has still not been filled. This gap is not a formatting issue. If the times of the card actions were used to fill in the early incident context, the later supplemental-recording time would be miswritten as the time the incident occurred, and the reason the original records have always needed to be retained would also be obscured.

Recovery actions and the root-cause investigation are not on the same track either. After the output directory was restored, the relevant paths could continue to be used; however, no explanation for the state discrepancy came with that restoration. The review lists the two separately so that the on-call records can acknowledge the recovery without treating the unconfirmed parts as completed.

## Attributions That Nearly Went Wrong

The initial intuition was to treat the difference as a problem with the current revision: the two entry points showed different revision values, which seemed sufficient to explain the two different states. This judgment was not ultimately adopted as the conclusion. The different revision values were merely an observation that coincided with the divergence, and could not establish which change triggered the state difference, much less establish that the compatibility bridge was necessarily involved.

Another approach that came close to being a mistake was to treat the restoration of the output directory as proof that the states were consistent. This did not hold up either. Recovery showed that one visible path was available again, but the core of this anomaly was that the same object was described as being in two different states at different entry points. As long as a provenance link was still missing between the original incident state and the current post-recovery result, recovery could not refute the earlier observations.

The third problem lay in a screenshot-based retelling. It had attempted to present the state more intuitively, but did not include the entry point, the current revision, or the location of the complete record. During the later review, the screenshot could not explain why the other path was working normally, nor could it establish which stage the displayed state belonged to. This retelling was retained as previously used material, but was no longer used for attribution.

The final risk came from subsequent summaries. Summaries compress multiple rounds of inspection into what looks like the latest result; this is usually useful for routine status pages, but in this incident it would allow post-recovery information to overwrite the first deviation. PLZC-011 isolated the first current revision entry after recovery precisely to preserve this boundary. Subsequent summaries can still be read, but cannot rewrite the original incident state.

## Uses of the retained materials

The materials for this incident are retained according to their purpose rather than according to "which looks more like the final answer".

| Material | Retained content | Questions it can answer | Questions it cannot answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original record | The two entry points, the state divergence, and the current revision seen at the time | Whether the divergence actually occurred | The root cause and duration of the divergence |
| Failure sample | Samples built around test | Why tiering and attribution were affected | Whether other objects were affected in the same way |
| Recovery page | The output directory restored to use | Which path became available again | Whether the two states have been explained |
| Current result | Subsequent status text | What someone saw later | How it corresponds to the original incident state |
| Handoff supplement | The first broken link and the need for confirmation | How far the investigation had progressed | The actual changes after the broken link |

This classification avoids two opposite kinds of loss. The first is retaining only the recovery page and consequently losing the failure state; the second is retaining only the initial anomaly and consequently losing visibility into which path has already recovered. Both types of material should be present, but they should not replace each other.

The Quality Signal Dashboard has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, and these arrangements help determine when the anomaly record can move from incident response to follow-up documentation. They do not constitute evidence of the cause. Exit criteria that only say "page restored" would be premature, because page availability and the ability to verify the source of the state are two different things; exit criteria that require a complete root cause to be found before the recovery record can be closed would also tie availability recovery to long-term attribution. The approach here allows the former to be recorded while leaving the latter open.

## Handling regression tiering

Regression tiering deals with failing samples, not abstract status labels. When a discrepancy appears, samples should still remain near their original tier, with their entry point and the current revision at the time attached. This is not about adding a lengthy explanation to every sample, but about retaining the minimum context needed for a valid subsequent review.

If all that remains for a sample is "pass" or "fail", it may look ready for a settled conclusion; but this incident shows that the conditions for reading statuses were not consistent. Moving it directly to the stable tier would disguise entry-point differences as changes in the sample's status. Conversely, there is no basis for permanently treating all related samples as unstable, because the material does not confirm whether they are reproducible. At this stage, the original tiering and dual-status annotations should be retained, without prematurely changing the nature of the samples.

Regression tiering records therefore need to distinguish three things: the original failing sample, the first current revision after recovery, and subsequent current results with no source attached. The first two have clear places in the incident; the third can only be treated as material pending linkage back to it. This distinction does not require creating a new set of tiers, only that these items not be merged into a single row when organizing the records.

## Handling the attribution of instability signals

Attributing instability signals depends on comparison: whether the same type of failure recurs under similar conditions, and whether a status can be traced back to an interpretable record. After different entry points returned different statuses in this incident, the conditions needed for comparison were no longer complete. Even if a later status seems closer to expectations, that does not justify classifying the failing sample as unstable or stable.

What can be done now is to bring attribution conclusions back down to the observation level. We can say: the object containing this failing sample exhibited two statuses; we can say: the output directory was later restored; we can say: the current results after recovery do not yet have a source attached. We cannot say: the two statuses have proved that a certain type of failure is unstable; nor can we say: the post-recovery status has proved that the earlier samples were old data.

The compatibility bridge remains among the unconfirmed items. It remains here because the early material already stated that "why the compatibility bridge changed is still unknown". No subsequent records have been added that could directly connect the change to the two statuses. Removing this item would mislead readers into thinking it had already been ruled out; rewriting it as a cause would go beyond the material. The most accurate status is still unknown.

## Recovery assessment

Recovery applies to the output directory, not the incident as a whole. After recovery, the path can be used again; this is a concrete recovery outcome. To avoid misinterpretation, the recovery page needs to retain this scope: state only that the output directory is usable, without extending that statement to consistency of the current revision, consistency between the statuses from the two entry points, or an unchanged compatibility bridge.

The record of the first current revision after recovery has value of its own. It is closest to the time of recovery and has not yet been overwritten by subsequent summaries. The backfill requirement in PLZC-011 to take only the first current revision starting from the time of recovery is intended to preserve exactly this. If the first record is missing, that absence should be explicitly retained, rather than replaced with a later summary.

For users, recovery means they can continue to perform the relevant operations through the restored output directory. For those maintaining the Quality Signal Dashboard, recovery means that on-site handling shifts from "path unavailable" to "status discrepancy pending attribution". These two assessments can both hold true, without either being written up as proof of the other.

## Specific gaps to fill in follow-up backfills

The information still to be added focuses on this anomaly itself, without expanding into a checklist for revamping the entire system.

- The two entry points where the two states were first seen, and the current revision corresponding to each.
- The timing of the first divergence relative to when the original record was saved.
- Whether the first current revision corresponding to the restoration of the output directory can still be retrieved.
- Whether the entry-point relationships missing from the current result can be recovered from the original record or the recovery page.
- Whether the first broken link that halted the handoff is on the execution-record side or the current-result side.
- Whether any changes to the compatibility bridge within that time window directly correspond to the state divergence.

Of these items, the first four are mainly for reconstructing record relationships; the fifth explains why the handoff could not continue; only the sixth could change the assessment of the compatibility bridge. Their order is not a commitment to a priority ranking, but is meant to keep an investigation into the cause from being written prematurely into the documentation of already verifiable incident details.

If supplementing the record turns up only one new current result but still no entry point or current revision, it only adds one observation and does not close the dual-state issue. If supplementing the record confirms that the state was the same before and after the output directory was restored, this only narrows the impact window and cannot by itself explain the cause of the initial divergence. If a change to the compatibility bridge is found but is not matched to an entry-point record, it must still be retained as a candidate rather than a conclusion.

## Current conclusion

This anomaly now has a clear recovery outcome: the output directory is usable again. There is not yet a root-cause conclusion. The Quality Signal Dashboard should continue to retain the original failure sample, the dual-state annotation in the regression tiers, the first current revision after recovery, and the gap in the current result's provenance.

The appearance of two states for the same object is not a display issue that can be eliminated with the last record. It reveals that the time of recording and the entry-point relationships were not saved together. Further documentation work can continue to fill timeline gaps, reconnect broken handoff links, and check the compatibility bridge, but until this material is in place, the recovery page and the cause page must remain separate.

## Order for reconnecting evidence during handoff

When taking over this incident record, do not start by choosing a current state that looks more credible. The verifiable starting point is still the two entry points in the original record, along with the current revision seen at each entry point at the time. The two must be copied back in pairs; copying only the state will lose the observation conditions again, while copying only the revision cannot show which state it corresponds to.

1. First, keep the original failure sample in its original tier, and attach the entry point for the first observation and the current revision at that time. At this stage, do not reclassify the sample as stable or unstable, and do not overwrite it with the post-recovery state.

2. Next, retrieve the first current revision after the point in the record when the output directory was restored. If only a later summary can be retrieved, mark the first record as missing; the later summary may be retained as corroborating evidence, but cannot substitute for the recovery point.

3. List the current result with no provenance separately. Only after its entry point and record location have been recovered can it be compared with the original incident state. Until its provenance is complete, it is neither proof of recovery nor proof that the dual-state condition persists.

4. Follow the handoff path recorded in PLZC-012 and stop at the first broken link, stating whether the broken link is on the execution-record side or the current-result side. What is needed here is a stopping point that can be located, not speculation about the cause of the broken link.

5. Only as the final step should you check whether there were any corresponding changes to the compatibility bridge within the same time window. If only one bridge change is found, with no entry-point record, it can still only be listed as a candidate explanation; only when the change, entry point, and revision can be aligned under the same recording conditions is there enough evidence to update the cause page.

After completing the linking back described above, the on-call team can assess two things separately: whether the output directory remains usable, and whether the source of the dual status has been explained. The former already has recovery records; the latter still depends on whether the missing entry-point, revision, and chain-break evidence has been supplied. The two conclusions should be saved separately to avoid merging them back into a single green or red status in the handoff summary.

This sequence does not require inventing absolute timestamps. The relative order remains the initial divergence, preservation of the original record, recovery of the output directory, the first record after recovery, the gap in source information, and the handoff stopping point. If precise clock data becomes available later, it should be linked back to the corresponding node as new evidence, rather than rewriting the timing gaps already faithfully preserved in earlier versions. Each supplementary entry must also specify whether the material comes from the original record, the recovery page, or the handoff record, and retain the corresponding entry point; if the material can only prove that the path is usable, keep it on the recovery side and do not move it to the cause page. If a record contains both recovery results and speculation about the cause, split it into two items and label each with its verifiable supporting evidence.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Exit Window Procedure

Capture the environment state before taking any exit actions. These checks cover the project's own exit path, the last directly visible result, and whether adj-fs has completed its exit. Release success still requires separate confirmation by the responsible owner; checkmarks on this list do not replace that confirmation.

## Before Opening the Window

- [ ] Open `docs/adj-fs/release/fs-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md` and verify the checklist version and this window.
- [ ] Retain the original input, the pre-change routing snapshot, and the first visible result. Cleaned-up green results must not overwrite the failure window.
- [ ] Keep one sample each for the normal path and the rejection path. Each sample must map to an object, a status, and an artifact version. If either path is missing, do not mark the window as ready to exit.
- [ ] Document the `.github/workflows` covered by this check, the build queue created by the release, the artifact version, and the rollback window. Exclude similar bypasses that do not belong to this project.

The "current result" must be tied to an object visible in the environment. If the logs say only "success" but the build graph has no corresponding artifact or status, treat the result as unconfirmed. If temporary diagnostics change the environment state, mark it as not comparable and keep a separate rerun record; do not replace the original sample with a post-diagnostic sample.

## Exit Sequence

1. First check whether the queue still accepts new work. If it does, stop; do not delete the original routing or continue cleanup.
2. Check the exit path against the pre-change snapshot. If old exit actions remain, delete only the actions that point to those old exit actions, and retain the snapshot; if the deletion scope is unclear, return to the snapshot rather than guessing from names.
3. Check the last visible result for the normal path and the rejection path separately, and record the object, status, and artifact version. Proceed to the next step only if the build graph's artifact or status matches what is visible in the environment.
4. After performing the exit action for adj-fs, remove the permissions and bypasses temporarily added for this window, and confirm that no new work is still coming in. If any of these cannot be confirmed, stop at this step.

## Stop Conditions

- Any mismatch in the checklist version, the environment's artifact version, or the routing snapshot: stop; do not overwrite the original input.
- Only "success" in the logs, with no build graph artifact or status: stop and wait for a visible result.
- A result for the normal path but none for the rejection path: stop; one path cannot stand in for completion of the window.
- Old exit actions cannot be distinguished, or deleting them would change the original failure window: stop and restore the pre-change snapshot.
- The exit action for adj-fs has been performed, but the queue still accepts new work: stop on the queue side; do not close the window.

## Rollback Records

When rolling back, restore the pre-change routing snapshot and retain the original failure window and object. Append recovery results only to `fs-quality-signal Exit Window Checklist`; do not overwrite the original record. Observations from PLZC-008 show that the execution record is dated earlier than the current result; a single "success" line cannot fill in the chronology. The card's 2026-02-02 record also handed the categorized issues to a new colleague working on integration testing; the handoff must therefore record the unfinished items actually taken over, not just say "the project team will keep an eye on it."

Keep the recovery result for PLZC-009 alongside the original failure window. A record that the recovery action is complete does not mean the original failure has disappeared; retain the object and respective result for both. Check temporary bypasses, permissions, and queue status as part of the same exit action as well; do not skip them just because the recovery result turns green.

## Closing the Window

- [ ] The exit action, last visible result, normal/rejection samples, and artifact version have all been recorded.
- [ ] The queue no longer accepts new work, and temporary permissions and bypasses have been removed.
- [ ] The exit action for adj-fs has been recorded; if independent confirmation of release success is not yet complete, leave it marked "unconfirmed" and do not close out the release prematurely.
- [ ] Unfinished items have been handed off to specific owners, with a clear record of the action where work stopped; vague statements about keeping an eye on things do not count as a handoff.

The early draft only said "find `remote action` first," "do not clean up the environment after you see the toolchain," and "stop here if `Rollback Window` does not appear," and also noted that the recovery action had not been tried in the shared environment. This version retains those operational hints but adds samples for both paths, queue stop conditions, snapshot-based deletion boundaries, and side-by-side records of recovery results.

# Quality Signal Console Approach Proposal

This draft preserves an approach that fs-quality-signal did not adopt at the time; it is not an active plan. The comparison focuses on two options: continuing with `sandbox helper`, or splitting out the generation entry point. Both remain options to try, with no start date and no handover arrangements that can be treated as already in effect.

## Assessment at the time

The initial working hypothesis was that splitting out the generation entry point would make quality-signal failure samples easier to classify. The reasoning was not that a generation entry point was inherently better, but that the two failure exits in `docs/adj-fs/proposals/not-adopted-fs-quality-signal-board-route.md` were different. If both remained under `sandbox helper`, it would be easy to treat different failure symptoms as the same type during replay.

The counterexample was straightforward too. With the existing helper, generation and execution at least still shared an entry point; after the split, that shared point could no longer preserve the original diagnostics for both sides. At the time, the active callers of the original diagnostics had not been confirmed, so "clearer after splitting" was only a preference, not enough to justify switching.

## Trial scope

If trials continue, use only what was left from the "unadopted fs · Quality Signal Board approach"—the original fs-quality-signal replay—as input; do not create more similar samples. Observe whether each of the two failure exits can leave a distinguishable record; do not judge solely by whether a replay finishes. If both the current entry point and the original revision are missing, leave the conclusion unknown rather than filling the gaps with guesses.

A trial should not also change other attribution paths for quality signals. This discussion is about whether the generation entry point should be independent, not about reorganizing all regression layers. That way, even if the split makes no difference, it will be clear which part to roll back, rather than treating the existing helper as a problem as well.

## Rollback point

The tentative rollback scope was to restore only the old entry point. That scope had not been finalized at the time either: if the original diagnostics actually depended on the generation entry point, restoring only the old entry point could leave incomplete records; if there was no such dependency, expanding the restoration scope would just mean making an extra change. The callers need to be found before this can be decided.

Related material continued to be maintained on its respective pages afterward; this draft retains only the comparison and unresolved points above. To check the original text, start with `docs/adj-fs/proposals/not-adopted-fs-quality-signal-board-route.md`.

# 2026.09 Compatibility Train Decision Record

2026.09 Cumulative Compatibility Train needs to address not an isolated build failure, but how long the old entry point should remain in place through this train and whether the adjustment window can be activated. The initial discussion presented the current target-model entry point and the adjustment window side by side: the former lets existing calls continue along the original path, while the latter would change the entry-point boundary and require callers to adapt to the new boundary.

The initial draft stated only the working assumption of "not switching directly". At that point, this statement was not yet sufficient to constitute a decision, because it did not specify what materials could turn a local result into a basis for comparison. After review, the assessment sequence was explicitly retained: first pin the same base revision, then retain the commands actually executed and the raw output, and only then follow the build graph to locate the first divergence. This sequence prevents results from different baselines, different commands, or summaries alone from being mixed together.

`src/remote/action.go` was an entry point used during the retrospective investigation. The search started with the terms target, base, cli, action, and sandbox, but this starting point does not mean the findings are permanently attributable to that file. If the first divergence is in the rules, continue investigating along the rule boundary; if the divergence is in CLI, remote action, or sandbox, the objects being compared change accordingly. Opening an action-related location first does not justify a decision to attribute all differences to remote action.

## Two Options

**Keep the current entry point.** The old entry point remains available, and callers can still run along the known path. Its immediate benefit is a smaller comparison surface: a trial run by the same caller can retain raw materials against a fixed baseline, without immediately layering entry-point changes on top of other build-graph changes. The cost is equally clear: the compatibility train will temporarily continue with the old entry point, and maintenance will require keeping track of both the path still in use and the adjusted path awaiting validation.

Retaining it does not mean the old entry point has been proven suitable for the long term. It simply postpones entry-point changes until a comparison is available. Without a caller trial run, "compatibility" describes only an expectation; it cannot show whether the caller actually passed through the adjusted divergence, nor can it show which state to return to during recovery.

**Enter the adjustment window.** This approach allows the entry-point boundary to be finalized earlier, and subsequent cleanup can proceed around the new window. The review did not treat it as an abstract desire for an upgrade, but as a concrete change that would affect existing call paths. The question it needs to answer is not "whether the change looks reasonable", but whether callers can perform a trial run under the same conditions and roll back if necessary.

The risks of a direct switch center on the lack of a basis for comparison. A completed build does not establish that an entry-point adjustment is safe: it may have used a different base revision, the commands may also differ from those on the old path, and if the raw output was not retained, it will later be impossible to determine whether the difference was caused by the entry point or by a baseline that had already changed. Worse, after a failure, rules, CLI, remote action, and sandbox would be conflated into a single line of investigation, making assessment difficult and leaving no clear reference for recovery.

The meeting materials therefore retained the adjustment window as a candidate rather than treating it as the default route. The old entry point cannot be retired until at least one caller has completed a reversible trial run. Here, "reversible" does not mean prior verbal agreement: before and after the trial run, it must be possible to refer back to the same base revision, actual commands, and raw output in order to compare behavior before and after the entry-point adjustment.

## This Round's Decision

This round's decision is to retain the current target-model entry point. The old entry point will remain in place until at least one caller completes a reversible trial run; this round approves only the scope covered by existing evidence and does not use the results of a single local run to extend the adjustment window to call paths that have not yet been observed.

This decision restricts the timing of the switch; it does not reject the adjustment window. The adjustment window remains a candidate, but it does not yet have evidence from actual use to support replacing the old entry point. If any of the caller trial run, divergence location, or recovery record is missing, the candidate must not be documented as a completed compatibility adjustment.

Review materials should be retained according to the relationships below. The branches in the diagram are not a division of responsibility; they indicate only where the assessment should pause and continue once the materials are complete.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Pin the same base revision] --> B[Retain actual commands and raw output]
    B --> C[Locate the first divergence in the build graph]
    C --> D{Divergence location}
    D --> E[Rules]
    D --> F[CLI]
    D --> G[Remote action]
    D --> H[sandbox]
```

The starting point in the diagram also explains why the approach of "adjust first, then look back for evidence" is unacceptable. If the entry point changes first, the output observed afterward already includes both the entry-point change and possible baseline differences; even if a difference is found, it is impossible to determine whether it was caused by the adjustment window. Conversely, only by first pinning the baseline and commands is it possible to map differences in the raw output onto the build graph and distinguish them.

## Approval Scope and Reservations

The current approval scope covers only the portions that can be compared using existing materials. It does not include callers that have not yet had a trial run, divergences that have not yet been located, or entry-point changes without recovery records. This scope may appear conservative, but it avoids treating compatibility as already established for unobserved branches.

The cost of retaining the old entry point has been accepted: there will be a period of parallel maintenance, and finalizing the adjustment window will also be delayed. The review did not choose to shorten this period by including all possible divergences at once. That approach prematurely merges the distinct boundaries of rules, CLI, remote action, and sandbox into a single window; it neither shows whether callers can roll back nor provides a comparable starting point if differences emerge later.

Another approach not adopted was switching immediately based on a single successful result. Its weakness is not that a successful result has no value, but that the result itself does not provide the complete conditions for comparison. If it is not possible to confirm whether the base revision is the same, whether the commands are the same, and whether the raw output is still available, success only shows that the path completed on that occasion; it does not support an entry-point decision for the entire compatibility train.

The reservations were therefore not pared down to the single sentence "we'll look at it later". The adjustment window is worth continuing to try, but the prerequisite is a reversible trial run by at least one actual caller. If a trial run provides only the final state, or cannot reproduce the same baseline and commands, it is still insufficient to change this round's decision; if the first divergence cannot yet be classified as rules, CLI, remote action, or sandbox, it should also remain unknown rather than being forced into a category just to advance the window.

## What to Retain During Review

Subsequent reviews will no longer record only "pass" or "fail". Each set of comparisons must at least allow a return to the same base revision, actual commands, and raw output, and identify where the first difference appears in the build graph. This does not add another process; it preserves a basis against which the adjustment window can be checked: without these materials, it is impossible to know whether the switch affects the entry point, rule behavior, CLI handling, or the boundary between remote action and sandbox.

For known divergences, the record should stop at the location where they were found. A rule divergence does not automatically extend to sandbox just because the word sandbox appears in the same investigation; nor should a CLI divergence be attributed directly to remote action on the grounds of an entry-point adjustment. Preserving localized assessments in this way allows subsequent caller trial runs to align with existing materials rather than being misled by earlier broad attributions.

`src/remote/action.go` can still serve as a lead for this retrospective investigation, but should not be treated as the sole entry point to the migration checklist. This decision concerns the trade-off between the target-model entry point and the adjustment window, and the comparison materials needed to support that trade-off; the code location is only a starting point for locating divergences in the build graph.

## Boundary with the Toolchain Handoff

The switchover handoff for the toolchain upgrade window is recorded in DOC-52. This page does not prescribe specific migration steps on behalf of that handoff document, nor does it treat progress in the toolchain window as evidence that callers have completed trial runs. What is recorded here is how the compatibility train handles the old entry point: continue to retain it, limit the approval scope, and wait for records of reversible runs by actual callers.

The initial draft presented "keep the current entry point" and the "adjustment window" as two options, while leaving the first divergence as an item to investigate. The reviewed draft made retention the decision for this round and added the sequence linking the same base revision, commands, raw output, and divergence location; the adjustment window remains a candidate and was not approved early based on expectations beyond the materials.

## Eligibility Records for Reopening the Window Next Round

When the adjustment window returns for review, the materials must be tied to an actual caller rather than merely adding a roadmap. The record should include together the old entry point used by that caller, the pinned base revision, the full commands, and the raw output; the candidate-path trial run must also state who performs the rollback and which old path is used to resume afterward. If any item is missing, this round's decision to retain the old entry point remains in effect.

The comparison should trace only as far as the first divergence in the build graph. If the divergence is in the rules, the rule side should continue verification; if it is at the CLI, remote action, or sandbox boundary, hand the complete preceding records to the corresponding owner. This page does not require a single trial run to explain everything downstream, nor does it allow a later summary of success to replace the first divergence.

The eligibility record can establish that the window meets the conditions for one reversible comparison, not that the candidate entry point is already fully compatible. Expanding the approval scope still requires specifying, one by one, which callers and boundaries the existing evidence covers; untested branches remain among the reservations.

During the upgrade window, do not replace the old installer-toolchain entry point directly with the candidate path. First list the callers still using the old entry point and record each caller's target label, current Please version, and whether they can roll back independently.

For the first round, choose only one consumer that can roll back on its own to try the candidate path. The handoff record must include a minimal BUILD snippet, the full command, and the output from the first failure; just writing "build failed" is not enough to determine whether the problem is in the toolchain, the target, or the caller's environment.

Keep the old entry point during the switch. Once the candidate path succeeds, migrate the registered consumers one at a time. At the first divergence, stop migrating on others' behalf and hand the target label, command, failure output, and recovery actions already tried to the actual owner.

If not all callers have been accounted for, or the rollback steps have not been documented, the status remains migration in progress.

# Please Toolchain Switch Handoff Procedure

This handoff covers the Please toolchain upgrade window, not an ordinary dependency replacement. The old entry point of installer-toolchain still has callers when the window begins; the candidate path is not a default that can simply replace the old entry point either. The two will coexist for a period, until all known consumers can switch from their own target labels and return to the original entry point if they fail.

The draft put "inventory callers" and "find one consumer to run through" in the same item. After review, they should be split: the inventory determines who will be affected, while the trial run determines whether the candidate path can be completed from a real consumer. Until the former is complete, one success should not be treated as a full switch; if the latter does not leave a rollback action, the first consumer should not bear the risk for subsequent callers.

## Build the handoff package first

Each handoff should provide a single package that the person taking it over can rerun. Do not use scattered screenshots from chat as a substitute. The package must contain at least the following items; if any item is missing, add it to the record before proceeding with the switch.

- **Target label**: Write the target label actually requested by this consumer. The toolchain target and the higher-level build target are not the same; seeing the toolchain succeed cannot substitute for the result of the consumer's target.
- **Please version**: Record the version used for the trial run. The easiest thing to confuse during the upgrade window is that the old entry point still works while the candidate path has only been validated under another version.
- **Minimal BUILD snippet**: Preserve the smallest snippet that causes the problem to appear or makes the candidate path take effect, and put it in the record verbatim. The snippet must be sufficient to show how the target connects to the toolchain; there is no need to bring in all unrelated rules.
- **Full command**: Keep the entire command, from entering the working directory through starting the build. If configuration overrides, the target label, or extra parameters are omitted, the person taking over may follow a different branch.
- **First failure output**: Preserve the earliest failure text; do not extract only the last line. A failure produced later during troubleshooting must not overwrite the original first-failure state.
- **Caller's rollback action**: Clearly state how this consumer restores the old entry point and which target it should rebuild after rollback to confirm recovery.

The handoff owner may add a line with the current assessment, such as "the candidate path started but failed before target resolution," but the assessment must be kept separate from the raw material above. The assessment may change; the target label, command, and first failure output should remain where they are. If the original assessment later turns out to be wrong, add a new result to supersede the assessment; do not delete the failure output to make the record look cleaner.

The following types of records are insufficient for a handoff: only stating "the new toolchain was used"; pasting a BUILD snippet without writing the run command; only saying "it can be rolled back" without the actual recovery method executed by the caller; or treating an unrelated successful target as validation. None of these can show what happened when the candidate path was used through this consumer's entry point.

## Start with the old entry point

The inventory starts with the known consumers of installer-toolchain and the old entry point, not with the implementation details of the candidate path. The list is granular at the caller level, not the directory level, and not at the level of a vaguely described class of rules that might be affected. One callerFang Ke can have multiple target labels; if their ways of connecting to the toolchain differ, record them separately.

Record at least three things for each item: which old entry point it currently uses, who can modify this invocation, and who can roll it back on their own during the window. Here, "self-rollback" means that the callerFang Ke restores the old entry point and reruns its own target; it does not mean that someone can later fix a global configuration elsewhere. Callers without rollback conditions do not enter the first batch.

The old entry point must remain available until the migration batch ends. This is not because the old entry point is more trustworthy, but to confine candidate-path failures to the current trial subject. If the inventory reveals a caller known only by name whose target label is unclear, explicitly mark it as unconfirmed in the list; do not guess a label to fill the gap. When the caller inventory is incomplete, this migration remains in progress; local trials are allowed, but the switch cannot be declared complete.

The inventory result does not need to become an organizational roster. Keep only the callers, entry points, and rollback conditions relevant to this window in the handoff. Newly added callers are not automatically counted within the migrated scope unless they enter the list with their own target labels and trial records.

## Select a trial subject that can roll back

Choose only one consumer for the first batch, and make sure it can roll back on its own. Record the reasons for selecting it: whether it has a clear target label, whether it can provide a minimal BUILD snippet, and whether it can restore the old entry point during the window. Do not skip these conditions because it is the easiest one to build; a successful result that does not resemble the real invocation method is of no help for the switch.

Before the trial run, run this consumer's target once through the old entry point, and put the Please version and full command used at that time into the handoff package. There is no need to archive every log from the old path; it only needs to be possible to identify whether the old entry point is still available and to give the post-rollback rerun the same baseline. Then switch the caller to the candidate path and build the same target.

When the candidate path fails for the first time, save the output first, then determine which divergence the failure occurred at. The first divergence is the earliest point after changing from the old entry point to the candidate path where execution can no longer continue, such as target integration, toolchain resolution, or build startup. Do not adjust the BUILD snippet, version, and invocation method at the same time just to get a pass; even if it succeeds, that will not show which change actually took effect.

If the failure is in the caller's own integration, hand it to the actual owner of that caller; if the material shows that the candidate path itself did not start as expected, retain the original output and return it to the toolchain maintenance side. The handoff only needs to pass along the first divergence; do not write a potentially unsuitable repair plan in advance for the person taking it over. While waiting for handling, this consumer restores the old entry point, and the other callers do not follow the switch.

A successful trial run only means that this consumer has completed the candidate path successfully. The record should identify the target label it completed and its rollback entry point. Do not rewrite "the first consumer succeeded" as "the old entry point has no consumers"; these two facts must be established separately by the inventory and migration records.

## Order of batch switching

Once the trial subject has completed and its recovery method has been retained, migrate the registered callers one at a time. Each caller repeats the same basic actions, but does not need to copy the previous caller's explanation: confirm its own target label and Please version, attach its own minimal BUILD snippet, run the full command, and retain its own first failure output or success result.

It is recommended that the window's status be written as brief lines rather than rewriting the process as a daily report:

```text
Caller:
Old entry point:
Candidate path:
Target label:
Please version:
Minimal BUILD snippet:
Full command:
First failure output or success result:
Rollback action:
Current status: not tried / in trial / migrated / rolled back / waiting for actual owner
```

"​​Migrated" may be entered only after the candidate path has completed the build for that caller and the rollback action has been written down. Even when no failure occurs, retain a brief description of the successful result; otherwise it will later be impossible to tell whether it was not tried, was omitted from the record, or was actually switched. "Waiting for actual owner" is not synonymous with failure; it means that the first divergence has been located at a boundary that someone can take over, but the caller has not yet completed migration.

Do not spread the same temporary change to other callers when one caller is blocked. First restore the current caller's old entry point, organize its minimal BUILD snippet, full command, and first failure output; whether the next item should be tried depends on whether it still meets the rollback conditions, not on whether the previous item went smoothly. This keeps the risk within a single caller instead of allowing an incomplete handoff to create a mixed state in which neither the old entry point nor the candidate path can be explained clearly.

## Restore the old path

Rollback should be a concrete action in the caller's record, not a promise from the toolchain maintenance side. Before starting the switch, the caller needs to know which old entry point to restore, which target label to run after restoration, and which command to use to confirm that it has returned to the original path. If it can only restore the configuration without rerunning the target, the rollback still cannot be considered verified.

A failure in the candidate path does not automatically mean that the toolchain upgrade must be abandoned altogether. First determine whether the failure belongs only to the current consumer's integration. If it belongs to the current caller, restore that caller and leave the handoff package; if the candidate path did not start or multiple registered callers hit the same divergence, pause the later batches and retain the old entry point as the available path during the window. Do not delete the trial records that already succeeded; they still show which integration methods have actually been exercised.

After restoration, set the status to "Rolled back" and attach the rerun result. Do not use "Issue handled" instead, because that would conceal the divergence that remains unresolved in the candidate path. When the person taking over provides a new result, append it below the original record; retain the old failure output and old assessment so it is possible to distinguish whether the same problem was fixed or the trial conditions changed.

## Handoff up to the first divergence

The handoff owner is responsible for assembling the entry point, target label, version, snippet, command, and first failure output into a usable incident context; the actual owner is responsible for handling a divergence with clear ownership. The boundary between the two sides is not determined by a generic "please follow up," but by whether the record shows when the failure moved from the old entry point to the candidate path.

If the first failure output has not yet been obtained, do not attribute the failure to the toolchain or the caller prematurely. If the target label is unclear, do not have the maintenance side guess based on the directory. First list the missing item under that caller and keep the migration in progress. A complete handoff package is more useful than a series of premature assessments, especially during a window in which the old entry point can still be rolled back.

This review retains one limitation from the draft: if either the caller inventory or the rollback action is missing, the page is not closed out. The new addition is the practice of saving the incident context and recovery result by caller, so later batches do not have to depend on the previous handoff owner's memory.
versions.change_summary: Separate the inventory, trial-run, and rollback records

# sandbox Static Linking Discrepancy Postmortem

During the verification window, the observed sandbox linking results still did not match the original plan. The discrepancy had initially been attributed to the toolchain, but that attribution was withdrawn after additional verification; this comparison did not provide enough support for it.

- When the discrepancy was first found, the window could not be cleared as planned. The failed command and exit code remain in the records from that window.
- The interim recovery action was to stop further approvals based on this result and narrow verification back to the sandbox linking checks; other completed checks were not rerun as a result.
- One additional verification was later performed for the same window. The discrepancy remained, but there was no new material that could pinpoint the root cause.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Static linking discrepancy first found] --> B[Stop approvals]
  B --> C[Perform one additional verification]
  C --> D[Root cause still unknown]
```

The surrounding platforms confirmed only their own boundaries as consumers or providers and did not extrapolate this discrepancy into a platform-side failure. The platforms do not explain sandbox's linking details on its behalf, nor do they change their own plans based on this single verification.

This is recorded only as a failed static linking verification, not as a basis for judging sandbox itself unusable. We still need a non-static comparison with the same input and to establish where the linker arguments are being pulled in from; until those gaps are filled, the root cause remains unknown.

# 2026.09 Compatibility Train On-Call Procedure

When a field report comes in from 2026.09 Cumulative Compatibility Train, don't rush to rebuild over and over. First save the version of cli-query, the raw results, and the log from the first build after the rollback. Get all three recorded first so later assessments have something Fang Ke to refer back to.

The handoff package must include at least:

- Target label
- Please version
- Minimal BUILD snippet
- Full command
- Initial failure output

Start with the first divergence. If you can confirm which target label, command, or BUILD snippet led to the observed behavior, hand off only that divergence to the relevant maintainer. Don't try to work out the full cause on the owner's behalf while on call. If fields are missing, collect the missing incident details first; if raw results are missing, don't substitute a cleaned-up account.

Stop if proceeding would require broader permissions, a change to public behavior, or deciding scope on behalf of the long-term owner. For cases that have already been rolled back, also include the log from the first post-rollback build in the handoff, and note which parts of this assessment are still unconfirmed.

### Still Open

The routing entry points for the relevant maintainers aren't listed together here. If both the target label and Please version are incomplete, stay at the evidence-collection stage; don't assign an owner based on similar symptoms.

# 2026.09 Compatibility Train On-Call Procedure

When 2026.09 Cumulative Compatibility Train has a report from the field, the on-call team saves the evidence first, then reruns. Do not reverse the order: once the raw cli-query results are overwritten by a new query, it becomes hard to distinguish the original behavior from changes caused by the rerun.

## Capture the evidence first

When a report comes in, save three things first:

1. The version of cli-query;
2. The raw results;
3. If a rollback has already happened, the log from the first build after rollback.

Keep the raw results as-is. You can add a brief note alongside them about what you see, but do not replace the pasted results with a cleaned-up summary. If the report only says "the train failed" without a target label, ask for the target label first; if the Please version is missing, ask for the version first; if the output from the first failure is missing, ask for that first. Until the materials are complete, do not infer the point of divergence from secondhand descriptions.

The minimum handoff package in the on-call record is:

```text
Target label:
Please version:
Minimal BUILD snippet:
Full command:
First failure output:
```

These five items describe the same incident. The minimal BUILD snippet should contain only the portion needed to reproduce this point of divergence; if you do not yet know which part is relevant, paste the snippet you received and mark it as unconfirmed. Do not delete key lines yourself just to make it "minimal." Keep the full command exactly as it was, including the argument order used at the time. Use the output from the first failure, not the output from the last retry.

## Follow the first point of divergence

Once all materials are available, first review the target label, command, and output from the first failure together. Address only the first point of divergence that can be confirmed directly from the incident materials:

- Target label does not match: send it back to the requester to supply the label; the on-call team must not substitute a similar-looking label;
- The BUILD snippet is not enough to locate the issue: request more of the snippet, or hand off the existing snippet marked "unconfirmed";
- The full command and output from the first failure are not from the same attempt: save them separately first; do not combine two attempts into a single record;
- Please version is missing: get the version first, then decide whether to rerun;
- A rollback has already happened: prioritize checking the log from the first build after rollback, and keep pre- and post-rollback materials separate.

"First" here does not mean the on-call engineer has to complete a root cause analysis. It only determines who gets the next set of materials and what is still missing. If you can identify the actual owner of the first point of divergence, send the complete handoff package to the corresponding maintainer and keep the raw results. If you cannot confirm the owner, stop at that point of divergence, record the target label, version, and missing information, and do not guess who is responsible based on similar commands.

## Reruns and stop conditions

Rerun only after the original materials have been saved. Use the full command from the handoff package. If the command needs to change for the rerun, write down the original command and the changes separately first. New results must not overwrite old ones, and the first build after rollback must also be saved separately.

The on-call team must stop immediately in any of these situations:

- Continuing requires broader permissions;
- Verification requires changing public behavior;
- You would need to decide the scope on behalf of the long-term owner;
- It is unclear which target label, Please version, or command the results correspond to;
- You are about to try again before saving the log from the first build after rollback.

Stopping does not mean clearing out the evidence. Keep the results already collected, and state in the handoff package which item you stopped at, which item is missing, and whether the first point of divergence has been confirmed. Mark anything unconfirmed as unconfirmed; do not fill gaps with "looks the same."

## Rollback scenarios

A rollback only changes the path for subsequent attempts; it does not delete the pre-rollback failure output. Save the pre-rollback raw results first, then the log from the first build after rollback. Put both under the same incident record, but clearly mark their order. If the first build after rollback still fails, hand that result to the corresponding maintainer first; do not keep expanding the scope of changes.

If the rollback has already produced usable results, do not take that as grounds to announce that public behavior has changed or that the long-term solution has been decided. The on-call record should only state what was observed in the first build after rollback, leaving decisions about changing public behavior to the actual owner. If the scope requires a decision from the long-term owner, apply the stop conditions.

## Include only local assessments in the handoff

Arrange the material for the maintainer in this order: target label, Please version, minimal BUILD snippet, full command, output from the first failure; keep the saved cli-query version and raw results in the same place, and attach the log from the first build after rollback if there was a rollback. Start with the first point of divergence, followed by the raw materials. If the first point of divergence is still unconfirmed, write "Unconfirmed" right at the start and list the gaps.

Do not turn guesses made during an on-call shift into long-term rules for the train. The on-call team can determine that "the target label is still missing" or "these two pieces of evidence do not come from the same attempt," but cannot make the call on public behavior. Do not rewrite failure output for convenience in the handoff, either; explanations can go on a separate line, but the original text must still be kept.

### Open point on this page

The specific contact points for the corresponding maintainers have not yet been collected in one place. For now, route the handoff to the actual owner based on the first point of divergence that can be confirmed from the incident. If even the actual owner cannot be identified, stop with the materials and gaps documented.
